docs.title: Agentic Engineering Patterns
docs.text:
Production agent systems fail in a way ordinary web apps do not: they return 200 OK and still give the wrong answer.

The process runs, the logs look normal, the stream closes cleanly — and the user gets a confident report about the wrong country, or a plan that executed twice, or an answer built on a number the model made up. This series is about that class of bug, and the handful of engineering patterns that prevent it.

It is written for an engineer who has built normal Python web APIs and is now looking at an agent system for the first time. You do not need to know LangGraph going in. You do need to be willing to ask one question of every code snippet: what was saved before this ran, and what is saved after? That question catches most silent failures.

docs.title: The one idea
docs.text:
Everything here turns on a single distinction:

  • Transport success — the request finished, nothing threw.
  • Semantic success — the right context, state, lock, plan, and persistence rules held.

A silent failure is any moment those two drift apart. Keep the Glossary open beside you; every term is defined there the first time it appears.

docs.title: How to read this
docs.text:
There is one path. Start at Chapter 1 and follow the Next link at the bottom of each page. The chapters follow the order you would build the system in, so read them as if you are implementing it. The two Bridge pages are short primers placed right before the pages that need them.

The appendix is optional. The glossary is worth keeping open beside you. The interactive lessons replay the same material as step-through decks. The source notes go deeper than the chapters and are best left until you have finished the main path.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Chapter 1 · Problem, design, and implementation plan — The production problem, what a deep agent is, the design principles, and the build order.
  • Chapter 2 · Designing a deep agent — You are asked to design a deep agent. The questions to ask, in order, and the principle that answers each one.
  • Chapter 3 · End-to-end architecture and orchestrator flow — The whole approve-to-worker run, end to end, before any piece is built.

docs.title: Build it step by step
docs.text:
• Step 1 · State and checkpoints — Give the agent memory that survives one request.
  • Step 2 · Context injection — Put the right user and business context at the right model boundary.
  • Step 3 · Planning and human approval — Make the agent show its plan before expensive work begins.
  • Step 4 · Identifiers that hold a run together — Name the run, plan, pause, attempt, event, lock tenure, and fact provenance correctly.
  • Step 5 · Streaming and background work — Let the user watch progress without letting the browser own correctness.
  • Bridge · DynamoDB conditional writes and SQS — The two AWS primitives the next steps lean on: conditional writes and FIFO queues.
  • Step 6 · Distributed locks — Make exactly one process own a run, even under double clicks, crashes, and retries.
  • Step 7 · Queue and worker execution — Move approved work out of the API process and make replay safe.
  • Step 7a · The event feed and idempotency — Make every progress frame appear exactly once, even after a crash and replay.
  • Step 8 · Orchestrator prompt — Decide what the prompt shapes and what code must enforce.
  • Step 8a · Reactive mode and its prompt — The one-pass contrast case: no plan, no approval, one prompt.
  • Step 8b · Clarifications — Handle ask-back turns without confusing source elicitation with plan approval.
  • Step 8c · Plan lifecycle — Decide when to replan, extend the locked plan, or skip planning.
  • Step 8d · Carryover and the data manifest — Reuse earlier results without pasting megabytes back into the context window.
  • Step 8e · Code components and organization — Split the code by ownership so every bug has an obvious home.

docs.title: Capstones
docs.text:
• Capstone 1 · Nine silent failures in one agent — Nine real bugs that returned 200 OK. Each should now feel recognizable.
  • Bridge · Evaluating an agent — What an evaluation measures, and the ways a passing score can still be wrong.
  • Capstone 2 · When the score passes and the work fails — Tool success that is not task success, and evaluations that hide a tradeoff.

docs.title: Appendix (optional)
docs.text:
• Glossary — Every term, defined once.
  • Appendix · Source notes — Optional full-depth design notes behind the chapters. Read after the main path, not instead of it.
  • Source note 1 · Before resume: the proposal turn
  • Source note 2 · The orchestrator: prompt, gate, and how to build one
  • Source note 3 · Life of a deep run

This is a teaching series. If a passage loses you, that is a bug in the writing — ask, and it gets fixed.

docs.title: Bridge · DynamoDB conditional writes and SQS
docs.text:
Steps 6 and 7 are built from two AWS services. DynamoDB stores the run's state, and SQS hands approved work to a background worker. Both steps assume you already know how these services behave when two writers collide or when a worker dies. This page teaches that behavior. The lock, the fence and the worker ritual come later.

The running example is the same retail analytics agent. A user asked for BRAND_A sales by market, approved a plan that queries SOURCE_A and SOURCE_B, and the run is now executing on thread abc.

docs.title: A DynamoDB item and its address
docs.text:
DynamoDB stores items. An item is a bag of named attributes, like a Python dict. Every item has an address made of two parts, the partition key and the sort key (PK / SK). The PK groups related items. The SK orders items inside that group. Together they name exactly one item.

This series uses two tables:

Table Holds Example address {env}-agent-events the run's feed lines, its run-state row, its run lock PK=abc, SK=12 is feed line 12 of thread abc {env}-agent-checkpoints the graph's saved state, and the resume claim PK=CLAIM#abc, SK=RESUME

DynamoDB enforces no schema beyond the key. So one table can hold several kinds of item, told apart by a prefix on the PK. In the events table, abc is the feed, run#abc is the run-state row, and lock#abc is the lock. Step 6 shows the full layout.

Writing an item looks like this:

import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("prod-agent-events")

table.put_item(Item={
    "PK": "abc",
    "SK": 12,
    "event": "Querying SOURCE_A for BRAND_A sales by market",
})

One fact about put_item matters more than any other. If an item already exists at that address, put_item replaces it completely. It does not merge, and it does not warn you. Whatever was in slot abc / 12 is gone.

docs.title: Why read-then-write races
docs.text:
Suppose two workers both think they should write feed line 12. The obvious way to avoid clobbering is to look first.

existing = table.get_item(Key={"PK": "abc", "SK": 12}).get("Item")
if existing is None:
    table.put_item(Item={"PK": "abc", "SK": 12, "event": my_line})

This is broken. Each line is a separate request, and the other worker can run between them.

worker A: get_item(abc, 12)  -> empty
worker B: get_item(abc, 12)  -> empty
worker A: put_item(abc, 12)  -> writes A's line
worker B: put_item(abc, 12)  -> overwrites A's line

Both workers checked, both saw an empty slot, and both wrote. A's line is lost and nobody got an error. The gap between the read and the write is the bug, and faster code or a retry does not close it.

docs.title: A conditional write closes the gap
docs.text:
A conditional write sends the check and the write as one request. DynamoDB evaluates the condition against the item currently at that address and applies the write only if the condition is true. It does both as one atomic step, so no other writer can act between them.

The condition goes in the ConditionExpression parameter. The most common one is attribute_not_exists(PK).

table.put_item(
    Item={"PK": "abc", "SK": 12, "event": my_line},
    ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(PK)",
)

Read it as "write only if no item lives at this address." The condition is checked against the one item at PK=abc, SK=12. It does not ask whether partition abc has any items at all. Every item has a PK, so "this item has no PK attribute" can only be true when the item does not exist.

Now replay the race. A's write finds the slot empty and succeeds. B's write finds A's item and is rejected. Exactly one worker wins.

Conditions can say more than "empty." expires_at < :now and claim_token = :token are both valid conditions, and Step 6 uses them. Values from your code go in ExpressionAttributeValues, with names that start with a colon.

docs.title: A failed condition is a normal outcome
docs.text:
When the condition is false, DynamoDB writes nothing and boto3 raises a ClientError whose code is ConditionalCheckFailedException. That error does not mean the database is broken. It means another writer got there first, and that is information your code asks for on purpose.

from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

try:
    table.put_item(
        Item={"PK": "abc", "SK": 12, "event": my_line},
        ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(PK)",
        ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure="ALL_OLD",
    )
except ClientError as err:
    if err.response["Error"]["Code"] != "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
        raise                              # a real failure: throttling, permissions, network
    occupant = err.response.get("Item")    # the item that was already in the slot

ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure="ALL_OLD" asks DynamoDB to put the existing item in the error response. Without it, you know you lost but not to whom, and finding out takes a second read. That second read reopens a gap, because the item can change before you read it. Step 6 inspects the returned occupant to decide what kind of collision it hit.

docs.title: TTL is cleanup, not a timer
docs.text:
DynamoDB can delete old items for you. You pick one Number attribute (this series calls it ttl), store a Unix timestamp in seconds, and turn on TTL for the table. A background process deletes items whose timestamp has passed.

That process is best-effort. It can delete an item long after its timestamp, and until it does, the expired item still shows up in reads and queries and still blocks an attribute_not_exists write. So TTL only keeps old rows from piling up. Any rule about time that your code depends on, such as "this lease has expired," must be a timestamp your own condition compares against the current time. Step 6 keeps these two fields apart on purpose.

docs.title: SQS FIFO in five behaviors
docs.text:
SQS is a message queue. The API sends a message, a worker receives it, does the work, and deletes it. This series uses a FIFO queue, whose name ends in .fifo. Five behaviors matter.

1. Message groups serialize work per thread. Every message sent to a FIFO queue carries a MessageGroupId. While one message from a group is in flight, SQS will not deliver the next message from that same group. Messages from other groups still flow to other workers in parallel. With MessageGroupId=thread_id, two runs of thread abc never execute at once, while threads abc and xyz run side by side.

import json

sqs = boto3.client("sqs")

sqs.send_message(
    QueueUrl=queue_url,
    MessageBody=json.dumps({"thread_id": "abc", "run_id": "run-001"}),
    MessageGroupId="abc",
)

FIFO queues also drop duplicate sends. Each message needs a deduplication id, or the queue can have content-based deduplication turned on, in which case SQS uses a hash of the body. A second send with the same id within five minutes is accepted but not delivered. Step 7 relies on this for double-clicked approvals.

2. Receiving a message hides it rather than removing it. When a worker receives a message, SQS makes it invisible to other consumers for the visibility timeout. The message is removed only when the worker calls delete_message with the receipt handle it got on receive. A worker that needs more time calls change_message_visibility to push the deadline out.

3. Silence means redelivery. If the timeout runs out before the worker deletes the message, SQS makes the message visible again and another worker receives it. SQS cannot tell a crashed worker from a slow one. It only sees that the message was not deleted in time.

4. SQS counts receives. Each delivery increments the message's ApproximateReceiveCount. A worker sees it only if it asks.

resp = sqs.receive_message(
    QueueUrl=queue_url,
    MessageSystemAttributeNames=["ApproximateReceiveCount"],
)
msg = resp["Messages"][0]
attempt = int(msg["Attributes"]["ApproximateReceiveCount"])   # 1 on first delivery

5. Too many receives sends the message to the DLQ. A redrive policy on the queue names a dead-letter queue and a maxReceiveCount. When a message has been received that many times without being deleted, SQS moves it to the DLQ instead of delivering it again. A FIFO queue's DLQ must also be FIFO. This stops one poison message from looping forever and blocking its group.

docs.title: At-least-once means replay-safe
docs.text:
AWS describes FIFO queues as exactly-once processing. That claim covers duplicate sends within the deduplication window. It cannot cover a worker that finishes half the work and then dies.

Walk through thread abc. The worker receives the message, queries SOURCE_A, writes three feed lines, and crashes before it deletes the message. The visibility timeout lapses. A second worker receives the same message and starts again. The SOURCE_A query runs twice, and the feed-line writes are attempted twice.

So from your code's point of view, every message can be delivered more than once. Any work a message triggers has to be safe to run again, with the same end state whether it ran once or three times. That property is idempotency. The queue will not give it to you. Your writes have to provide it, and conditional writes are the main tool for that.

docs.title: What Steps 6 and 7 build on top
docs.text:
You now have every piece the next two steps assemble.

Step 6 · Distributed locks turns attribute_not_exists plus an expiry condition into a claim that only one process can hold. It then guards every renew and release with a condition on a per-tenure token. Its write fence is the conditional put on a feed slot from this page, with ALL_OLD used to tell a harmless replay from a zombie writer.

Step 7 · Queue and worker execution uses MessageGroupId=thread_id for one worker per thread and extends the visibility timeout on each checkpoint as a heartbeat. It copies ApproximateReceiveCount onto the run-state row and treats the DLQ as the only path that pages a human. Because redelivery means replay, it gives every feed line an idempotency key that comes out the same on the second attempt.

Next: Step 6 · Distributed locks.

docs.title: Bridge · Evaluating an agent
docs.text:
Every page so far tested the agent the way you test a web API. You call it, check that nothing threw, and check that the right rows landed in the right table. That catches infrastructure bugs. It cannot tell you whether the agent picked the right data source or answered the question the user asked. For that you need an evaluation. Capstone 2 assumes you know what one is and how one can mislead you. This page covers that much.

The running example is the same retail analytics agent. A user asks a question about BRAND_A, the agent plans which of SOURCE_A through SOURCE_D to query, and it answers with figures from the rows it got back.

docs.title: Transport success is not task success
docs.text:
The series turns on one distinction, transport success versus semantic success. A request that finished with 200 OK has transport success. A run where the right context, state and plan held has semantic success.

Evaluation applies the same split to the agent's output. The run finished, the tool returned rows, and the answer streamed. All of that is transport success, and your logs and tests already see it. Task success means the user got what they asked for, built from the rows the agent retrieved and not from the model's memory. The series calls that rule grounding. An agent that queries SOURCE_A when the question needed SOURCE_C has transport success and fails the task. So does an agent that writes a paragraph about a table instead of returning the table.

Nothing in the infrastructure can see that second kind of failure. Only an evaluation can.

docs.title: What an eval is
docs.text:
An evaluation, or eval, has three parts.

A dataset of cases. Each case is an input plus a statement of what good output looks like. The input is often a question and some seeded conversation state. Each case has a stable id, so you can find the same case in next week's run.

case = {
    "id": "brand_a_canada_q3",
    "question": "BRAND_A sales by market in Canada, last quarter",
    "expected_sources": {"SOURCE_C"},
    "expected_behavior": "answer",      # or "clarify" when the question is ambiguous
}

A grader. A grader is a function that takes one case and the agent's output and returns a verdict. The verdict can be pass or fail, a number, or a label such as correct, incorrect or clarify.

A score. The score summarizes the verdicts across the dataset, for example "82% correct."

The dataset says what you care about, and the grader says how you check it. The score is the part people read, and it is also the part with the least information in it.

docs.title: Two kinds of grader
docs.text:
Code-based graders check something a program can decide. Did the agent choose exactly the expected sources? Does every figure in the answer appear in the rows it retrieved? Did it return a table when one was asked for? These graders are cheap and fast, and they give the same verdict every time. They can only check what you can state precisely.

def grade_sources(case, run) -> str:
    return "correct" if run.sources_called == case["expected_sources"] else "incorrect"

LLM-as-judge graders hand the case, the agent's output and a rubric to a second model and ask it for a verdict. Use one when the property is real but hard to write as code. Examples are whether the answer addresses the question that was asked, or whether it says plainly that SOURCE_B has no Canada coverage. A judge can read meaning, which code cannot. It also has its own failure modes. Its verdict can change between runs. It can favor answers that are long, fluent or confident. And it grades only what you show it. A judge that sees the answer but not the retrieved rows cannot tell whether a figure was read from data or made up. It will often pass a plausible-looking number.

Use code where the check can be stated exactly, and a judge only for what is left. Before you trust a judge, read a sample of its verdicts next to the outputs it graded, so you know it checks the thing you meant.

docs.title: What a score can hide
docs.text:
A score is an average, and an average throws information away. Four kinds of loss come up again and again.

The average hides a category. Say the dataset has 80 single-market questions and 20 cross-market questions. A change lifts single-market accuracy from 85% to 95% and drops cross-market accuracy from 70% to 40%. The overall score rises from 82% to 84%. It reports a small win and hides a large regression in one slice of the dataset.

The score grades a decision but not the artifact. A grader that checks "did the agent call SOURCE_C?" says nothing about whether the answer used SOURCE_C's rows correctly. A high score on the decision says little about the output.

The verdict buckets hide a tradeoff. If clarify and incorrect both count as "not pass," then an agent that stops asking questions and starts guessing can raise the pass rate. Some of those guesses are right, and the rest turn into confident wrong answers. The pass rate went up while the agent got less honest. You only see this if you keep the verdicts apart.

The two runs did not test the same cases. If cases were added or removed between runs, or expected labels changed, the two scores came from different datasets. Comparing them tells you about the datasets as much as the agent.

A judge can add a fifth problem on top of these. It can grade the wrong property consistently, and the score will look stable and trustworthy while measuring something nobody asked for.

docs.title: The minimum evaluation loop
docs.text:
A small loop beats a large dataset that nobody reads. For an agent, the minimum is:

  1. Fix the dataset. Version it, give each case a stable id, and record where each expected label came from.
  2. Run every case, more than once if you can. The same agent can answer the same question two ways, so a single run per case mixes noise with signal.
  3. Grade each case and keep the per-case verdicts. Store case_id -> verdict, not just the mean. Every analysis below needs the per-case rows.
  4. Compare against a baseline on the same cases. Restrict to cases present in both runs with unchanged labels. Count how many moved from each verdict to each other verdict, rather than subtracting two averages.
  5. Read the failures. Open the transcripts of the cases that changed. The transcripts show why a verdict changed, and the score cannot.
  6. Add a case for every production failure. When a user hits a bug, turn it into a case before you fix it. If the bug comes back, that case fails.

Steps 3 and 4 are the ones teams skip, and they are what Capstone 2 is about.

docs.title: What Capstone 2 builds on this
docs.text:
Capstone 2 · When the score passes and the work fails takes these ideas into a real system. Part 1 lists nine failures where the tool succeeded and the task did not. Part 2 grades decisions and artifacts separately, and pairs cases across two snapshots. It then builds the verdict transition table from step 4 and finds a drop in clarifying questions that turned into confident wrong answers. It also checks where the labels came from and whether the holdout set was really held out. Part 3 shows how to design an experiment when you want to claim that one specific change caused an improvement.

Next: Capstone 2 · When the score passes and the work fails.

docs.title: Capstone 1 · Nine silent failures in one agent
docs.text:
Design question: How do I fix it for real? · Principles: Fix Root Causes, Attack the Premise, Exhaust the Design Space

Use this as the final review exercise: a deep agent can look healthy, return 200 OK, and still be wrong.

Capstone. This is where the series lands: the nine bugs below are the failure modes from the build path (state, context, planning, identifiers, streaming, locking, durability, and prompt boundaries) seen together in one real system. Each bug recalls its mechanism in a few lines and links back to the step that teaches it.

This article is written for the engineer who has built normal Python APIs and is now trying to understand production agents. If that is you, the hardest adjustment is this: with agent systems, "the request succeeded" is not the same as "the work was correct."

We learned this while building a commercial-strategy agent that helps commercial leaders answer where-to-play, what-to-play and how-to-win questions. The agent takes a question, proposes a multi-step research plan, pauses for human approval, then executes the approved plan and writes a report. On paper, the stack was ordinary enough: LangGraph for orchestration, middleware for context injection, DynamoDB for persistence, and Server-Sent Events for streaming progress to the browser.

Before one release, code review found nine bugs. None crashed the app. None produced scary logs. None would have paged anyone. Each one completed successfully while corrupting the meaning of the run.

That is the core lesson of this piece:

Transport success means:
  the HTTP request finished

Semantic success means:
  the right context, state, lock, plan, and persistence rules all held

Deep agents fail when those two meanings drift apart.

docs.title: The system in plain English
docs.text:
Imagine a business user asks:

Give me my sales.

That sentence is not enough by itself. The system needs to know what "my" means: which country, which product, which time period, and which previous conversation context should carry forward.

So the agent does four things:

  1. It adds user-specific context before the model sees the question.
  2. It asks the model to propose a research plan.
  3. It pauses and waits for a human to approve or refine that plan.
  4. It resumes later, runs the research, streams progress, and saves the final answer.

The hard part is that these steps do not happen inside one neat function call. A single user turn spans multiple HTTP requests, may resume on a different API replica, and depends on checkpointed state in DynamoDB.

None of the bugs below are "the model hallucinated" stories. They are ordinary engineering bugs at the boundaries around the model.

The bugs use the series' terms as they were taught: thread_id, state, checkpoint, interrupt(), Command(resume=...), plan_id and claim_token. Each is defined once in the Glossary.

docs.title: The architecture: one user turn, several HTTP requests
docs.text:
Most backend systems map one user action to one request. Deep mode does not. A single research turn spans at minimum three separate HTTP requests over potentially 30 or more minutes:

POST /chat/stream?mode=deep        <- proposal: fresh question, starts the graph
  -> streams plan as SSE
  -> closes at "interrupt" frame (graph pauses, no "end" sent)

POST /deep/{thread_id}/plan/refine <- optional: user wants changes
  -> Command(resume={type: refine, feedback: "..."})
  -> streams updated plan, closes at "interrupt" again

POST /deep/{thread_id}/approve/async <- user locks the plan
  -> validate plan_id + interrupt_id
  -> stage resume decision in checkpoint
  -> write run-state queued
  -> enqueue FIFO message
  -> return 202 queued

GET /deep/{thread_id}/events       <- browser watches research
  -> tail curated event log until run-state completed/failed

These are independent HTTP requests, potentially from different browser tabs, different API replicas, and minutes apart. The graph does not know they are related. LangGraph's checkpointer does.

docs.title: How the checkpoint ties them together
docs.text:
Every LangGraph node that runs writes its output to the checkpoint. When submit_plan calls interrupt(), the graph pauses and LangGraph writes the interrupt payload, including the plan, the prompt, and gate metadata, to the checkpoint's pending writes. The HTTP request finishes, the SSE stream closes, but the graph state is frozen in DynamoDB, waiting.

# gate.py - submit_plan tool
decision, feedback = _decision_of(
    interrupt({
        "kind": "plan_approval",
        "thread_id": thread_id,
        "owner_id": owner_id,
        "plan": plan.model_dump(),
        "prompt": prompt,
    })
)
# Everything above interrupt() re-runs on every resume.
# Everything below runs only after the human decision arrives.

The plan is therefore stored twice for practical purposes:

  • As graph state in the plan channel, so later graph nodes can read it.
  • As part of the pending interrupt payload, so the HTTP approval endpoint can validate the exact plan before resuming.

That is why read_pending_gate(thread_id) can see gate["plan"]["plan_id"] before the graph resumes. It is reading the pending interrupt metadata from the checkpoint, not recomputing the plan.

On the refine or approve request, read_pending_gate(thread_id) reads the interrupt payload directly from the checkpointer, with no graph compile required, to validate preconditions. A refine request may synchronously resume to produce another plan. In the production approve path, the endpoint stages the approval decision into the checkpoint, writes run-state as queued, enqueues a FIFO message, and returns 202 queued.

# deep.py router - approve endpoint
gate = read_pending_gate(thread_id)
if gate is None:
    raise HTTPException(404)
if gate["plan"]["plan_id"] != payload.plan_id:
    raise HTTPException(409, "plan_id_mismatch")

persist_resume_decision(thread_id, {"type": "approve"})
put_run_state(thread_id, run_id, status="queued")
enqueue_deep_run(thread_id, run_id)
return {"status": "queued", "run_id": run_id}

The plan_id and interrupt_id checks prevent a stale browser tab from approving an older pause after the user has refined it. plan_id may identify the logical plan across refinements; interrupt_id identifies the exact interrupt the user saw.

Tab A sees plan_id p1
Tab B refines plan to p2
Tab A clicks approve with p1
API reads pending gate p2
API returns 409 plan_id_mismatch

Later, the worker receives the queue message and calls agent.astream_events(None, config). The approval is not in the SQS message and not in an ordinary state channel; it is already staged in checkpoint pending writes.

docs.title: Why the checkpoint and the resume claim live in the same DynamoDB table
docs.text:
LangGraph does not support concurrent runs on a single thread. Two approve clicks racing, or two browser tabs both hitting approve, would execute the research plan twice and leave the final checkpoint to whichever process finished last. To prevent this, we write a claim item to DynamoDB before every resume:

DynamoDB table: agent-checkpoints
|- Checkpoint items  (LangGraph's own PK/SK scheme per thread + step)
\- Claim items       PK = "CLAIM#{thread_id}", SK = "RESUME"
                     Fields: claim_token, expires_at, ttl

Both live in the same table because the claim needs the same durability and region as the checkpoint, and an in-process claim would be invisible to other API replicas. It is the acquire-with-expiry, token-guarded-release claim from Step 6. Bug 8 below is what happened before release checked the token.

docs.title: One Langfuse trace across all three requests
docs.text:
Each graph.astream_events() call opens a new LangGraph run, which by default opens a new Langfuse trace. Without intervention, a deep turn that goes proposal -> refine -> approve produces three sibling traces with no structural link. We seed the trace ID deterministically from the thread ID:

trace_id = langfuse_client.create_trace_id(seed=f"deep:{thread_id}")
handler = CallbackHandler(trace_context={"trace_id": trace_id})
handler.last_trace_id = trace_id

Same thread_id means the same seed, which means the same trace ID on every request. All three phases land in one Langfuse trace, one Agent Graph, properly sequenced.

In Langfuse terms, a trace is the top-level timeline for one logical user task. A run or observation is one child operation inside that timeline, such as a LangGraph invocation, model call, tool call, or chain step.

CallbackHandler is the bridge that receives LangChain/LangGraph callback events and sends them to Langfuse. Passing trace_context={"trace_id": trace_id} tells it to attach this request's events to the existing logical trace.

Langfuse trace: deep:t-123
  run: proposal request
    model call
    tool call submit_plan
  run: refine request
    model call
    tool call submit_plan
  run: approve request
    model calls
    research tools
    report writer

Without the seeded trace ID, those three HTTP requests look like unrelated traces. Debugging "why did this approved plan produce that report?" becomes a manual correlation problem.

docs.title: The design: state channels and middleware
What a LangGraph channel is
docs.text:
Each state key is a channel with its own update rule. The default, LastValue, keeps the old value when a turn does not write the key, and Step 1 explains why that is a footgun for channels that must reset on a new turn. messages uses an appending reducer instead.

Persisted channels in our agent included:

messages          DeltaChannel    Full transcript: HumanMessage, AIMessage, ToolMessage
todos             LastValue       [{content, status}] managed by write_todos tool
plan              LastValue       Serialized Plan dict: plan_id, status, steps, modification_count
entity_groups     LastValue       [{country, brand, period}] written by submit_plan
raw_question      LastValue       User's verbatim question text
user_context      LastValue       Rendered context block (defaults + memory)

docs.title: Why we split state across two TypedDicts in two files
docs.text:
LangGraph compiles the graph state schema from state_schema= plus any state_schema fields declared by middleware. We used that to co-locate each channel declaration with its sole writer:

# gate.py
class DeepState(DeepAgentState):
    plan: NotRequired[dict[str, Any]]
    entity_groups: NotRequired[list[dict[str, Any]]]

# proposal_context.py
class _UserContextState(AgentState):
    raw_question: NotRequired[str]
    user_context: NotRequired[str]

# graph.py
graph = create_deep_agent(
    ...,
    state_schema=DeepState,
    middleware=[UserContextMiddleware(), ...],
)

At compile time, LangGraph merges DeepState and _UserContextState into one checkpointed schema. At runtime they are indistinguishable, but in the source each channel declaration sits beside the code that writes it. Dropping UserContextMiddleware from the middleware list still compiles and runs. The channels just disappear from the checkpoint quietly, the same kind of structural gap Bug 5 exploited.

docs.title: Why middleware for context injection
docs.text:
We needed to prepend user-specific context, including defaults and prior conversation entities, to the user's question before it hit the model. Four approaches were on the table:

  • System prompt injection: rejected because the orchestrator prompt is request-invariant and cached.
  • Checkpointed message injection: rejected because the block would accumulate in history across turns.
  • Tool call: rejected because it adds an extra model/tool round trip and can be skipped.
  • Middleware: inject just before the LLM call, after the checkpoint is read.
class UserContextMiddleware(AgentMiddleware):
    state_schema = _UserContextState

    def wrap_model_call(self, request: ModelRequest, handler):
        return handler(self._inject(request))

    async def awrap_model_call(self, request: ModelRequest, handler):
        return await handler(self._inject(request))

    def _inject(self, request: ModelRequest) -> ModelRequest:
        context = str((request.state or {}).get("user_context") or "")
        if not context:
            return request
        ...
        return request.override(messages=messages)

request.override(messages=...) returns a new ModelRequest. It does not mutate state. The injected copy vanishes after the model call, the checkpoint stays clean, and the middleware reads its own declared channels directly from request.state.

The tradeoff is that the injection is invisible in the checkpointed transcript and every assumption the injection code makes about message structure becomes a correctness risk. Bugs 2 and 3 are both examples of those assumptions failing.

docs.title: 1. Injected context kept overriding a decision the user already made
docs.text:
Middleware injected the user's default entities, country Australia, on every model call, including execution calls after a human had approved a plan for Germany. The model resolved Germany correctly at plan time, so this is neither Step 1's stale state nor Step 2's plan-time precedence bug. During execution the freshly injected default sat near the top of the prompt while the approval sat lower in history, and the report came back about Australia. Gating injection on plan status would have broken multi-turn sessions, so the fix was a precedence rule written into the context block and the execute step. Step 8 steps through the bug and shows the shipped prompt text.

Lesson: when context should only apply at one phase of a multi-phase pipeline, encode that constraint in the context itself. A prompt rule beats a code gate when the code gate has to reason about shared state across turns.

docs.title: 2. A framework dependency swapped in a synthetic HumanMessage under our feet
docs.text:
The context middleware attached its block to the latest HumanMessage in the request. deepagents installs a summarization middleware unconditionally, and near the context limit it replaces old history with a synthetic HumanMessage tagged lc_source: "summarization". The original user message may already be gone. Our reverse scan found the summary, attached the context to it, and so labeled summarizer prose as the user's own words. The fix skips messages with that tag. Step 2 shows the corrected scan.

Lesson: when your code finds "the latest item of type X in a list," enumerate every party that can insert an X. Framework middleware can insert objects that pass isinstance(msg, HumanMessage) without being genuine user input.

docs.title: 3. A search loop continued past its target and decorated the wrong message
docs.text:
The injection code scanned backward through the message list looking for a HumanMessage with string content. The original condition:

if isinstance(msg, HumanMessage) and isinstance(msg.content, str):
    # inject here

LangChain messages can carry list-form content for multimodal inputs (images, documents). If the latest human message has list content, the condition fails and the loop keeps going backward until it finds an older string message.

Message list (newest at the bottom):

  index 0  HumanMessage  "Give me Germany sales"     ← Turn 1 (string content)
  index 1  AIMessage     "Here are the results..."
  index 2  HumanMessage  [image, "Compare these"]    ← Turn 2 (LIST content, fails check)

Backward scan starts at index 2:
  index 2 → HumanMessage but content is list → FAIL → keep going
  index 1 → AIMessage → skip
  index 0 → HumanMessage with string → MATCH → inject here ✗ WRONG TURN

Turn 2's context ("user defaults: Australia") gets injected into Turn 1's question. Turn 2's message receives no context at all. The model plans for Australia when the user asked about Germany, and the context lands on a turn that already completed.

The fix was to separate "not the target" from "the target exists but cannot be processed":

for i in range(len(messages) - 1, -1, -1):
    msg = messages[i]
    if not isinstance(msg, HumanMessage):
        continue
    if msg.additional_kwargs.get("lc_source") == "summarization":
        continue
    if not isinstance(msg.content, str):
        logger.warning(
            "user_context not injected: latest human message has %s content",
            type(msg.content).__name__,
        )
        return request
    # inject and return

Lesson: in a backward search, failing the capability check should not silently retarget the search to an older item. When you find the right item but cannot act on it, stop and log.

docs.title: 4. User-influenced text inside a trusted block could forge its own closing delimiter
docs.text:
The context block closes with [/User context], and part of the block comes from session summaries we do not fully control. If that text ever contained the literal delimiter, it would close the block early and the rest would pose as the user's words. The fix lowercases the delimiter inside injected text before embedding it. Step 2 shows what the model sees with and without the escape.

Lesson: this is prompt injection. Any time you embed external text inside a structured format that uses delimiters, escape your delimiter before embedding.

docs.title: 5. A three-file invariant had no structural owner and no error on violation
docs.text:
Starting a new turn required writing three LastValue channels together: the message, the raw question, and the context block, even when the context is empty. The rule lived in a hand-built dict in one file, the channel declarations in another, and the readers in a third. A caller that wrote only messages would silently keep the previous turn's raw_question and user_context. The fix was a factory function, build_proposal_graph_input, placed beside the channel declarations. This is the France/Germany bug from Step 1.

Lesson: there is a hierarchy of invariant enforcement: type signature, factory function, documented convention, and tribal knowledge. Critical invariants should sit as high in that hierarchy as practical.

docs.title: 6. The post-stream database write got cancelled when the client hung up
docs.text:
A deep run streamed its end event and then awaited the database save. The frontend correctly closes the SSE connection as soon as it sees end, and in Starlette a client disconnect raises CancelledError at the generator's next await. The save never ran. Because CancelledError is a BaseException in Python 3.11+, no except Exception block logged it. The fix starts the save as a background task before yielding end. Step 5 shows the before and after.

Lesson: any await inside an SSE generator that runs after a terminal event is a race against client disconnect. Create the task before yielding the terminal event and hold a strong reference to it.

docs.title: 7. Writer and reader used different keys for the same record
docs.text:
Chat history is stored in DynamoDB under chat_id. The approval payload marked chat_id as optional.

The writer used a fallback:

key = payload.chat_id or payload.session_id

but every reader used only chat_id:

history = get_history(payload.chat_id or "")

When the frontend omitted chat_id, the write succeeded under session_id. The next reader looked up "" and found nothing. Deep mode looked stateless for that traffic slice with no error anywhere.

Quick mode had already solved this correctly by skipping the write entirely when chat_id is absent:

if not chat_id:
    logger.info("skipping persistence: no chat_id")
    return

Lesson: if a field is optional, some callers will omit it. Writer and reader must handle that absence identically. Otherwise you create rows that no reader will ever find.

docs.title: 8. The lock release did not prove it still owned the lock
docs.text:
The resume claim expires after 30 minutes, and the run deleted it on completion with an unconditional delete_item. A run that outlived its lease could therefore delete a second request's newer claim and reopen the double-run window. The fix stores a per-claim token on acquire, makes release conditional on it, and logs a skipped release at info level. That is the token-guarded delete in Step 6.

Lesson: "release a lock" and "release your lock" are different operations. Always prove ownership on release.

docs.title: 9. Embedding stateful context in message records made an explicit reset invisible
docs.text:
After each completed turn, we saved session state, including resolved entities such as country, brand, and time period, as a field on the assistant message record in DynamoDB. The next turn scanned message history in reverse to find the most recent record with that field and injected it as context.

The bug was a three-step collapse of semantics.

First, the state field was coerced before storage:

entity_groups = values.get("entity_groups") or None

An explicit reset to [] became None.

Second, the persistence layer skipped None fields:

if md.entity_groups:
    item["entity_groups"] = md.entity_groups

The reset turn was written with no entity_groups attribute at all.

Third, the read path scanned backward for the most recent non-empty value:

for msg in reversed(memory):
    groups = msg.get("entity_groups", [])
    if groups:
        return groups

So the scan skipped the reset turn and landed on an older populated turn, rehydrating stale state.

The fix was to move session state out of message records and into a purpose-built store with direct overwrite semantics:

state_value = values.get("session_state")
if state_value is not None:
    store.put(session_id, state_value)

state_value = store.get(session_id)

None means the state channel was never set and the previous row remains untouched. [] means explicit reset and should overwrite the previous value.

Lesson: embedding session state inside event or message records creates two structural problems. It forces readers to scan history instead of doing direct lookup, and it makes empty-vs-absent semantics easy to destroy through convenience coercions like x or None.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
All nine bugs shared one property: the code ran to completion and the operation succeeded in the narrow transport sense because nothing threw. What failed was the semantic contract.

Bug What "succeeded" What happened Context overrides approved plan 200 OK, report generated Report about wrong entities Synthetic message targeted 200 OK, context injected Context labeled summarizer prose as user words Loop retargeted wrong message 200 OK, context injected Context attached to a previous turn's message Delimiter forged in block 200 OK, plan proposed Smuggled text treated as user content Convention-only channel write 200 OK, turn started Previous context bled into a new turn Save cancelled on disconnect 200 OK, end event sent Database write never ran Wrong key on write 200 OK, row written Row written under a key no reader uses Unconditional lock release 200 OK, claim deleted Another request's claim was deleted [] or None reset invisible 200 OK, turn answered Follow-up planned against prior topic entities

The review habits that caught these before they shipped were consistent:

  • Test the content, not just the return code.
  • Read library source, not just the docs.
  • For every abstract pattern, such as injection, locking, or persistence, enumerate failure modes phase by phase and ask whether a transport-level success code means the semantic work completed.

Built on LangGraph, Python 3.11, DynamoDB, and Starlette SSE. The stack is incidental. Context injection targeting, lock ownership, async cancellation, and writer-reader key mismatch are universal failure classes.

docs.title: A note on the approval code snippet
docs.text:
One detail to watch in the approval endpoint pattern above: the code shows a plan_id check, but plan_id is stable across refinements by design: it names the logical plan, not the exact interrupt. To reject a stale browser tab that approved an older revision, also validate interrupt_id, which is minted fresh for each pause:

gate = read_pending_gate(thread_id)
if gate is None:
    raise HTTPException(404)
if gate["plan"]["plan_id"] != payload.plan_id:
    raise HTTPException(409, "plan_id_mismatch")
if gate["interrupt_id"] != payload.interrupt_id:
    raise HTTPException(409, "interrupt_id_mismatch")
# only now stage the decision
persist_resume_decision(thread_id, {"type": "approve"})
put_run_state(thread_id, run_id, status="queued")
enqueue_deep_run(thread_id, run_id)
return {"status": "queued", "run_id": run_id}

plan_id catches a plan-content mismatch. interrupt_id catches the more common case: the user refined and re-interrupted, but an old tab still has the original interrupt open.

You should now understand

  • How the same 200 OK shape appears across state, context, streaming, locking, and persistence bugs
  • Why the useful review question is semantic: "did the right invariant hold?", not only "did the request finish?"
  • Why stale state, stale browser tabs, stale lock holders, and stale memory records are the same family of production problem
  • Why each earlier chapter exists: every build step prevents one class of silent failure in this case study
Final review

Pick any one bug in the table above. Name the chapter that should have taught you to catch it, the invariant that failed, and the smallest test or review question that would expose it.

Example answer

For "unconditional lock release," the chapter is Step 6 · Distributed locks. The failed invariant is: a process may only release the claim it still owns. The review question is: "Does release prove ownership with the current claim token, or does it delete by thread id alone?" The test is a takeover scenario: A acquires, A's lease expires, B acquires, A attempts release, and B's claim must remain.

docs.title: Four more from production (post-release)
docs.text: The nine above came from a single pre-release review. These four arrived as production PRs in the following weeks. They follow the same pattern: the system reported success, and something semantic was wrong.

docs.title: Quadratic writes from replace-semantics streaming
docs.text:
A model that emits reasoning tokens sends many thinking.delta events, each carrying the full accumulated reasoning text to that point (replace semantics). Persisting each delta naively means N deltas write O(N²) bytes into one DynamoDB partition key, which hit the per-partition write-capacity ceiling (~1,000 WCU/s) mid-run.

The fix: time-coalesce live frames in the curator, flushing at most once per 2 seconds per step. The SSE path to the browser stays byte-identical; only the durable-log write is coalesced.

The lesson: replace-semantics streaming plus per-delta persistence is quadratic. Identify the semantics (append vs. replace) before deciding whether to persist every frame or the last.

docs.title: Async client bound to a per-job event loop
docs.text:
Each worker job called asyncio.run(), which creates and closes a new event loop per job. A cached httpx.AsyncClient is bound to the event loop that created it; on the second job, the first client's loop is already closed, and the first Cortex call dies with Event loop is closed.

The fix: one process-lifetime asyncio.Runner, with pooled clients drained at shutdown. A weakref guard converts any reintroduced per-job asyncio.run() into a named error at startup.

The lesson: an async client must never cross event loops. In a worker process that runs many jobs, one process-lifetime runner is the only safe design.

docs.title: Burned timeout retried
docs.text:
ReadTimeout was classified as a retryable error, so a call that already spent its entire 300-second timeout budget was replayed for another 300 seconds. Two exhausted attempts burned 600 seconds on work that had no chance of succeeding faster.

The fix: only retry errors that fail before the request was sent (ConnectError, ConnectTimeout), plus rate-limit and gateway responses (429, 502, 503). Use jittered exponential backoff. A ReadTimeout means the server acknowledged the request and timed out during processing; retrying it from the start sends a duplicate with no guarantee the first copy was not processed.

The lesson: a burned timeout is spent budget, not a transient blip. Classify retryable errors at the transport layer, not at the exception class.

docs.title: Stale plan re-persisted on a follow-up turn
docs.text:
The plan channel is LastValue. The exit path persisted the plan onto every completed turn's DynamoDB record, including follow-up turns that never called submit_plan. This caused a stale prior-turn plan to be stamped onto a follow-up row and resurface later as the current plan.

The fix: stamp plan.minted_run_id = deep_run_id at plan creation and persist only when plan.minted_run_id matches the current turn's deep_run_id. Fail open when either is absent.

The lesson: a sticky LastValue channel written only at plan time, combined with end-of-run persistence on every turn, silently re-persists the old value. The turn's own run id is the only safe discriminator.

Next: Bridge · Evaluating an agent covers the evaluation basics Capstone 2 assumes. Capstone 2 then moves up one layer, to tool results that aren't task results and evaluations that hide a tradeoff.

docs.title: Capstone 2 · When the score passes and the work fails
docs.text:
Design question: What does done mean? · Principles: Explain the Number, Prove It Works, Test Behavior, Not Implementation

The first capstone was about code that returned 200 OK while corrupting the meaning of a run. This one is about the same failure one layer up: an evaluation that passes while the agent's work is wrong, and a tool call that succeeds while the user's task does not.

Capstone. Read Capstone 1 · Nine silent failures in one agent first. That article is about infrastructure: state, locks, keys and persistence. This one is about the contract between the model, its tools and the evaluations we use to judge it. The system is the same commercial-strategy agent; every name below is generic.

The lesson from the first capstone was:

Transport success:  the HTTP request finished
Semantic success:   the right context, state, lock, plan and persistence rules held

This article adds two more lines:

Tool success:       the tool returned without error
Task success:       the user got the thing they asked for, built from real evidence

Score success:      the evaluation passed
Behavior success:   the agent made the right decision and said so honestly

Every failure below lives in one of those gaps.

docs.title: Part 1 · Nine more silent failures, at the model–tool contract
docs.text:
These came from production traces and regression tests after the first capstone shipped. In each case the infrastructure was correct: the right context reached the model, the run completed, the stream closed cleanly. What failed was the agent's behavior or the contract around it.

Failure What "succeeded" What happened Output-language instruction never reached the model Language detected, answer streamed Answer came back in the default language New topic inherited old scope Follow-up answered Previous entities and filters applied to an unrelated question Source asked a question; parent swallowed it Tool returned success The source needed clarification; the user never saw the question Clarification answer routed to the wrong agent Answer delivered User chose a source inside one agent; a different agent with the same name was called Artifact described instead of delivered Answer streamed The agent wrote about the table it would build; no table arrived Column acknowledged but not rendered "Added the column" The artifact was unchanged Inline numbers not read from stored rows Answer contained figures The figures were never read from the retrieved data Right sources, wrong query shape Source-set check passed A cross-scope question was sent as one combined query instead of one per source One source's context leaked into another's query Both sources answered Market-specific context filtered a regional query

docs.title: 1. Diagnose the boundary before blaming the model
docs.text:
The output-language failure looked like a weak model ignoring an instruction. It wasn't. Language detection worked, but its result never reached the prompt the model received.

The review habit: before you call something model behavior, read the exact prompt at the model boundary. In a tracing tool such as Langfuse, open the generation span, not the request span. If the instruction isn't there, it's an infrastructure bug, and no amount of prompt wording will fix it.

The fix had three parts: propagate the detected language into the loop prompt, state it near the opening and again after the answer-format rules, and add a regression test that asserts the instruction is present at the boundary.

A caution about what that fix proves. Propagation, wording and placement all changed in one change. It's tempting to say "moving the instruction later fixed it," but placement's own effect was never isolated. The defensible claim is the boundary test, not a placement result. (Part 3 shows how you would test placement properly.)

docs.title: 2. A successful tool status is not a successful task
docs.text:
Three failures share one root: the system treated "the tool returned" as "the task is done."

  • The swallowed question. A data source sometimes returns a question instead of rows ("Which sales source: vendor or internal?"). The tool call succeeds. If the parent agent treats any non-error result as data, the question disappears and the agent answers from nothing.
  • Described, not delivered. Asked to show a table, the agent wrote a paragraph describing the table. The model produced text; the turn completed.
  • Acknowledged, not rendered. Asked to add a column that already existed in the data, the agent said it had added it, and returned the unchanged artifact.

The fix is a contract, not a better prompt:

def handle_source_result(result, step):
    if result.kind == "question":
        # Relay to the user, tied to the source that asked and the open step.
        return Clarification(asked_by=result.source_id, step_id=step.id,
                             question=result.question)
    if result.kind == "rows":
        return Evidence(source_id=result.source_id, rows=result.rows)
    raise UnexpectedResult(result)

For artifacts, separate two kinds of follow-up:

  • Presentation-only changes (sort, relabel, chart type) may rebuild from rows already held.
  • Data-changing requests (new rows, new values, a different filter) must retrieve. A fail-closed guard rejects a "rebuild" that claims to change data without a retrieval in the same turn.

We learned the second rule the hard way: an earlier filter-to-rebuild shortcut let the render path keep every row while the answer claimed the filter was applied.

docs.title: 3. A clarification answer belongs to whoever asked
docs.text:
A third-party data vendor appeared twice in the system: as a source inside the sales agent, and as an agent of its own. The sales agent asked "vendor or internal?" The user said "vendor." The orchestrator matched the word and routed to the vendor agent.

Nothing in the infrastructure was wrong, and the provenance metadata in the orchestrator's own context showed the mismatch. The model bound the answer to the wrong referent by name.

The fix: a clarification relay that records who asked and which plan step is open, and routes the answer back to that asker. The model can still phrase the question; code decides where the answer goes.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OpenClarification:
    asked_by: str      # source or agent id that asked
    step_id: str       # plan step waiting on the answer
    question: str

def route_answer(answer: str, pending: OpenClarification) -> Dispatch:
    # Never re-route by matching names in the answer text.
    return Dispatch(target=pending.asked_by, step_id=pending.step_id, user_choice=answer)

The general rule: the scope of an answer is set by the question, not by the words in the answer.

docs.title: 4. Context is per-source, not per-turn
docs.text:
Two failures came from context with the wrong scope:

  • Inherited scope. A new, unrelated question picked up the previous turn's entities and filters. The carryover rules were written for follow-ups and applied to everything.
  • Cross-source contamination. Context meant for a market-specific source (a country, a local metric definition) was injected into a regional source's query.

Both fixes are the same shape: resolve scope per turn (is this a follow-up or a new topic?) and inject context per source, not as one blob for the whole request.

docs.title: 5. Grounding means reading, not retrieving
docs.text: The agent quoted figures inline after a retrieval step, but never read them from the stored rows. Retrieval happened; reading didn't. The action contract now requires a stored-row read before any number is quoted. An evaluation that only checks "did the agent retrieve?" would never catch this.

docs.title: Score decisions and artifacts separately
docs.text:
Our routing evaluation grades the agent's first decision: which sources it would call. It doesn't execute retrieval or check the final answer. That is useful and cheap, but it measures the orchestration contract, not the truth of the answer.

A passing tool-choice score can hide an unchanged table (failure 2). So keep two scores:

Score Question it answers Example Decision correctness Did the agent choose the right action? Right sources, right mode, retrieve vs rebuild Artifact correctness Did the user get the right result? Table changed, figures match stored rows

Report them separately. A rise in one is not a rise in the other.

docs.title: Compare the same cases, not two summaries
docs.text:
Between two evaluation snapshots, the non-pass rate fell by more than half. It looked like a clean win. It wasn't, for two reasons:

  1. The case sets differed (new cases were added, sources changed), so the two summaries weren't comparable.
  2. "Non-pass" counted clarifying questions as failures.

Restricting to the cases present in both runs with unchanged expected labels, and looking at each verdict separately, told a different story:

Verdict on the same cases Before After Correct ~70% ~82% Wrong but confident ~10% ~15% Asked for clarification ~20% ~3%

Correctness improved, mostly because the agent asked less. But some cases that used to ask now answered confidently and wrongly. The uncertainty didn't go away; it stopped being disclosed.

A transition table over paired cases shows this:

from collections import Counter

def transitions(before: dict[str, str], after: dict[str, str]) -> Counter:
    """before/after map case_id -> verdict ('correct', 'incorrect', 'clarify')."""
    shared = before.keys() & after.keys()
    return Counter((before[c], after[c]) for c in shared)

# The cell to watch: ('clarify', 'incorrect') — questions that became confident errors.

The rule: never report an improvement from two unpaired summaries. Pair the cases, split the verdicts, and look at the transitions. The safety-relevant change often hides in one off-diagonal cell.

docs.title: Know where your labels come from
docs.text:
Check three things about your labels:

  • Who wrote the expected labels. Ours are engineering-authored or derived from rules in the question banks, not independent expert consensus. That's fine for regression; it's not ground truth.
  • Whether the holdout is really held out. Our file called "holdout" deliberately includes questions that also appear as prompt examples. That makes it regression coverage, not a generalization test.
  • Which cases are known-open. Some cases are flagged as known failures so they're still scored but don't fail the build. An unexpected pass should force someone to remove the flag, not pass silently.

docs.title: Check the shape, not just the set
docs.text: "Did the agent pick the right sources?" is a set comparison. It misses a cross-scope question sent as one combined query when it should have been one query per source. Add query-shape assertions for the cases where shape matters.

docs.title: Part 3 · Claims you can and can't make
docs.text:
Production changes rarely isolate one variable. In one release, propagation, wording and placement of an instruction all changed together. You can claim "the instruction now reaches the model, and a test enforces it." You can't claim "placement fixed it."

If you want to know whether placement matters, design the experiment:

  1. Freeze the instruction text, model, settings, tools, access and seeded conversation state.
  2. Ensure the instruction reaches the model in every condition, so missing propagation can't masquerade as a placement effect.
  3. Vary only the location (opening, after format rules, latest turn, a structured state block).
  4. Randomize order, repeat each case several times, and score with rules declared in advance.
  5. Report paired changes and regressions with uncertainty, on cases that weren't copied from prompt examples.

docs.title: Part 4 · Telemetry you shouldn't trust
docs.text:
• Missing negative feedback is not success. Most users don't click thumbs-down. Silence is not a score.
  • Cost fields can be empty. Most of our deep-run traces reported zero cost. Treat a field as evidence only after checking it's populated.
  • Attribution from traces is often impossible. When we tried to classify user-reported failures as model or infrastructure from traces alone, most stayed ambiguous. If you can't tell from the outside, you need the system (or the model) to record why it did what it did.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
Failure class What looked fine What to check instead Boundary Instruction in the code Instruction in the prompt the model received Tool vs task Tool returned success Result kind: rows, question, or error Artifact Answer streamed Artifact changed; data changes retrieved Relay Answer delivered Answer routed to the asker, not a name match Scope Follow-up answered Scope resolved per turn, context injected per source Grounding Retrieval happened Numbers read from stored rows Evaluation Score went up Paired cases, split verdicts, transitions Labels Holdout passed Holdout independent of prompt examples Telemetry No complaints, zero cost Fields populated; silence isn't success

Review habits that would have caught these earlier:

  • Read the prompt at the model boundary before blaming the model.
  • Treat every tool result as a typed value (data, question, or error), never as "not an error, so data."
  • Score decisions and artifacts separately.
  • Pair evaluation cases and read the transitions, especially "used to ask, now confidently wrong."
  • Write down what a change proves and what it doesn't.

The stack is incidental. These are failure classes of any agent that calls tools, asks questions and gets judged by a score.

docs.title: Chapter 1 · Problem, design, and implementation plan
docs.text:
Start with the problem, not the framework.

A user asks a business question. The system should produce a sourced research report. Before it calls expensive tools, a human should see and approve the plan. The work may take forty minutes. The browser may disconnect. A worker may crash halfway through. A second worker should resume without duplicating the report.

That is the system we are building in this series.

The agent inside it is a deep agent: one that drafts a multi-step plan, waits for a human to approve it, then carries it out over many tool calls and many minutes. Its working state lives in a database, not in one process, so the run can pause and resume. The contrast case is a one-pass agent that calls a tool once and answers, which this series calls reactive mode (Step 8a).

The whole system is a distributed system with an agent inside it. A chatbot or an API handler that calls a model and returns never has to survive a crash halfway through a forty-minute job.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
A crash is the easy failure, because you can see it. The dangerous one looks like this:

HTTP request: 200 OK
Logs:         normal
User sees:    plausible report
Reality:      wrong country, duplicated work, stale context, or invented number

This is the distinction the whole series turns on:

Transport success:
  the request finished

Semantic success:
  the right context, state, plan, lock, persistence, and provenance rules held

An ordinary API often lets you treat those as the same thing. A production deep agent does not.

docs.title: The design decisions
docs.text:
Six decisions shape the implementation. Chapter 2 argues each one as the answer to a design question, so here they get one line each.

  1. Make state durable, so a run survives a different request, worker, or deploy. See what the nouns are and what states they can be in.
  2. Inject context at a controlled boundary. See where the boundaries are.
  3. Plan before execution, with a human approving the plan. See where the human comes in.
  4. Name every moving part. See what the nouns are.
  5. Separate progress from truth. See what happens when two things happen at once.
  6. Use code for boundaries and prompts for judgment. See where the boundaries are.

docs.title: The implementation plan
docs.text:
We will build the system in this order:

Chapter 2   Designing a deep agent: the questions to ask
Chapter 3   End-to-end architecture and orchestrator flow
Step 1      State and checkpoints
Step 2      Context injection
Step 3      Planning and human approval
Step 4      Identifiers
Step 5      Streaming and background work
Bridge      DynamoDB conditional writes and SQS
Step 6      Distributed locks
Step 7      Queue and worker execution (7a: the event feed)
Step 8      Orchestrator prompt (8a to 8e: reactive mode, clarifications,
            plan lifecycle, carryover, code layout)
Capstones   Nine silent failures; when the score passes
Identifiers make more sense after you have seen a plan pause and resume. Locks make more sense after the browser can double-click approval. Prompt design makes more sense after code already owns the boundaries.

docs.title: The lifecycle of a single run
docs.text:
Here is the full system we are going to build:

flowchart LR
    A[Question] --> B[Context<br/>injection]
    B --> C[Orchestrator<br/>drafts plan]
    C --> D{Human<br/>approval}
    D -->|approved| E[Queue<br/>FIFO]
    E --> F[Worker<br/>picks up]
    F --> G[Graph runs<br/>step by step]
    G --> H[Checkpoint<br/>after each step]
    G --> I[Streamed progress<br/>→ browser]
    H --> J[Final report<br/>persisted]

Here is what happens at each stage and what can go wrong at each boundary.

Question. The user's intent arrives as text. It is not yet enough to act on. The agent also needs to know who the user is, what they are permitted to see, and what defaults apply to their account.

Context injection. Before any model call, the system attaches what the model cannot derive from the message alone: account context, user permissions, locale, relevant business rules. The system has to keep "what the user typed" and "what the system added" apart on purpose. Step 2 covers this.

Orchestrator drafts a plan. The model reads the enriched question and produces a structured sequence of steps a human can read and evaluate: "query this source, verify that figure, draft this section" instead of "do research." Step 3 covers this together with approval.

Human approval. The plan pauses at a gate. A human reads it and approves or rejects it. Only after approval does any expensive execution begin. This single gate means the run spans two or more HTTP requests, not one. Step 3 covers this.

Queue. The approved plan is handed to a FIFO queue, keyed on the conversation thread. The API process returns immediately; the queue holds the intent durably until a worker is ready. Step 7 covers this.

Worker. A background worker dequeues the job and begins executing the plan. The worker is independent of the API process. It may run on a different machine, across a deploy boundary, or restart after a crash without the user knowing anything changed. Step 7 covers this.

Graph runs step by step. The worker runs the plan as a LangGraph graph, one node per step. Each node reads from state, does its work, and writes results back. Step 1 covers how that state works.

Checkpoint after each step. After every node, LangGraph persists a checkpoint: a complete snapshot of state at that point. If the worker crashes at step 4, a new worker reads the checkpoint and resumes from step 4 instead of starting over. Step 1 covers checkpoints.

Streamed progress → browser. As the graph runs, it emits progress events over SSE (server-sent events). The browser shows the report being built section by section. The SSE connection is ephemeral, and closing the browser must not stop the work. Step 5 covers this.

Final report persisted. When the graph completes, the finished report is written to durable storage. The user can reload, share the link, or return a week later.

docs.title: What makes this a distributed system
docs.text:
Each stage of the lifecycle runs in a different context:

  • The API process handles the question and the approval.
  • The queue holds intent across process boundaries.
  • The worker executes the plan.
  • The checkpoint store persists state across crashes and deploys.
  • The SSE stream connects the browser to live progress without keeping the work alive.

The standard tutorial loop (call model, run tool, return answer) never shows this. When work must outlive the request that started it, you are no longer writing a request handler. You are operating a small distributed system, and every boundary between those components is a place where state can be lost, duplicated, or corrupted while every individual component still reports success.

The rest of this series covers how to prevent the 200 OK, wrong-answer failure at each of those boundaries.

docs.title: Terms you'll meet
docs.text:
Chapters 2 and 3 use these words before the steps that teach them. One sentence each is enough to keep reading. Each links to its glossary entry and names the page that teaches it properly.

  • Deep agent. An agent that plans, pauses for approval, then executes over many steps with its state in a database. Defined above.
  • Checkpoint. The saved copy of the graph's state after each step. Any process can reload it and continue the run. Taught in Step 1.
  • Interrupt. The interrupt() call that pauses the graph to wait for a human. The pause is written into the checkpoint, so the HTTP request can end. Taught in Step 3.
  • SQS FIFO queue. An AWS queue that will not hand out a second message for a conversation while the first is still being worked on. That gives one worker per conversation. Introduced in the DynamoDB and SQS bridge, used in Step 7.
  • DynamoDB and conditional write. DynamoDB is the AWS database that holds checkpoints, run-state, locks and events. A conditional write succeeds only if a condition is true at that instant, so two racing writers get exactly one winner. Introduced in the bridge, used for locks in Step 6.
  • Worker. A background process that takes an approved run off the queue and executes it, separate from the API process that handled the request. Taught in Step 7.
  • Carryover. Reusing what an earlier turn already resolved or retrieved, instead of asking or querying again. Taught in Step 8d.
  • Data manifest. A short index of the results the agent already holds, shown to the model in place of the data itself. Taught in Step 8d.

You should now understand

  • The production problem this series solves
  • Why a deep agent is a distributed system with an agent inside it
  • The design decisions that shape the implementation
  • The step-by-step build plan for the rest of the chapters
  • Why 200 OK and "the work was correct" are not the same thing
Try this

Your team builds a request handler that calls an LLM, lets it pick tools, and returns the result, all in one HTTP request. They want to add human approval before any expensive tool runs. A colleague says: "Easy, just interrupt the function, wait for the approval callback, then resume." What breaks with that design, and what has to change?

Answer

The approval can take minutes or days, because a human reads and approves asynchronously. Holding an HTTP connection open that long is not possible in practice (timeouts, load balancers, client disconnects). Approval changes the system topology: the first request produces the plan and returns; the human approves out-of-band; a second request resumes the run. This requires (1) durable checkpointed state so any replica can pick up the run, (2) a pause mechanism (interrupt()) that serializes the graph to storage rather than blocking a thread, and (3) a separate resume endpoint that delivers the human's decision. The single-function model doesn't survive crossing an HTTP boundary.

Next: Chapter 2 · Designing a deep agent — you have been handed this problem; work out the questions to ask before drawing any boxes.

docs.title: Chapter 2 · Designing a deep agent
docs.text:
You have been asked to build an agent for a retail business. Commercial leaders will ask it multi-step sales questions, such as "compare BRAND_A sales in Germany and France, and tell me which channel drove the gap." It answers from four data sources, SOURCE_A through SOURCE_D, licensed per market. One requirement is fixed from the start. A human approves the research plan before anything expensive runs, because the plan spends real money on queries.

Chapter 1 set out the problem. Runs take forty minutes, browsers disconnect, workers crash, and the worst failures return 200 OK with the wrong answer. This chapter is the thinking you do before you draw a single box.

The method is to ask questions in the order a careful engineer would ask them. Each question has a tempting first answer. For each one you will see what that answer broke in this agent, the decision that replaced it, and the engineering principle behind the decision, with a small example from the real code. Each section ends with the Step where you build the answer. By the end, the twelve answers add up to the architecture in Chapter 3.

Twenty-four principles come up along the way. You do not need to memorize them. They are what you reach for when a question has no obvious answer, and each one gets a one-sentence definition where it first appears.

docs.title: What does "done" mean, and how will I know?
docs.text:
Start here, because every later answer gets checked against this one.

The tempting answer. Done means the run finished. The endpoint returned 200, the stream closed, and a report arrived. You write tests that call the endpoint and assert a non-empty report.

What goes wrong. In this agent, a run with a clean 200 produced a confident report about Australia when the user asked about France. The evaluation side had the same problem one layer up. Between two evaluation snapshots, the non-pass rate fell by more than half, and it looked like a clean win. When the team paired the cases that appeared in both runs and split the verdicts apart, clarifying questions had dropped from about 20% to about 3%, and wrong-but-confident answers had risen from about 10% to about 15%. The agent had not become more certain. It had stopped saying when it was unsure.

The decision. Write down three layers of "done" before writing any code:

Transport success:  the request finished, nothing threw
Semantic success:   the right context, state, plan, lock and persistence rules held
Task success:       the user got what they asked for, built from retrieved rows

Then build the checks that can tell the layers apart. That means tests that read back state across turns, and an evaluation with stable case ids and per-case verdicts that you compare as pairs.

Explain the Number. Before you trust or act on a number you measured, name what limits it and rule out everything else it could be measuring. The "non-pass rate halved" number was measuring two things at once. The case sets differed between snapshots, and the clarify verdict was counted as a failure. The fix keeps every verdict and compares only shared cases:

def transitions(before: dict[str, str], after: dict[str, str]) -> Counter:
    shared = before.keys() & after.keys()
    return Counter((before[c], after[c]) for c in shared)

# The cell to watch: ('clarify', 'incorrect'), questions that became confident errors.

The same habit applies to performance numbers. When reasoning-token streaming started failing mid-run, the limiter had a name, DynamoDB's per-partition write ceiling of about 1,000 WCU per second. Persisting every replace-semantics delta wrote O(N²) bytes into one partition. Once you could name the limiter, the fix followed from it. The curator now coalesces live frames to at most one write per two seconds per step.

Test Behavior, Not Implementation. A test claims what the code's users can observe, so it should fail when that behavior breaks and keep passing when only the internals change. Step 1 asks for one test that catches a whole class of bug. A second turn passes empty context and asserts that nothing from the first turn survives. In sketch form:

run_turn(thread, "sales in Germany", user_context="default country: Australia")
state = run_turn(thread, "sales in France", user_context="")
