assert state["raw_question"] == "sales in France"   # state a caller can read back
assert state["user_context"] == ""

It reads checkpointed state, which any later request will see. It does not assert which helper built the input dict.

Prove It Works. Check the real artifact, not a proxy or a self-report. One production failure looked like a weak model ignoring an output-language instruction. Language detection worked. The instruction never reached the model. The habit that found it was opening the generation span in the trace and reading the exact prompt the model received, rather than the request span or the code that was supposed to build it. The regression test now asserts that the instruction is present at the model boundary. The same discipline applies to telemetry. Most deep-run traces reported zero cost, and that field became evidence only after someone checked it was populated.

Where you build it. The evaluation bridge teaches the minimum evaluation loop. Capstone 2 applies it to this agent.

docs.title: Do I need a deep agent at all, and what is the smallest thing that works?
docs.text:
Now that you know what done means, ask how little machinery gets you there.

The tempting answer. The approval gate is the safe path, so every message goes through it. Every turn writes todos, submits a plan, pauses, and waits for approval.

What goes wrong. Many turns are not new questions. A user answers a source's ask-back ("in-store or online?"), adds a market ("also pull New Zealand"), or asks to re-sort a table. If those turns reopen the gate, the system mints a new plan_id. Evidence in this agent is filtered by plan_id, so the results already fetched drop out of the current cycle, and the human is asked to approve the same question twice. The opposite mistake costs as much. A one-pass agent that calls a tool and answers cannot survive a forty-minute job or a human pause.

The decision. Build two modes. Reactive mode is a one-pass router:

decide -> call at most the needed data tool once -> answer

Deep mode is for runs where planning, approval, attribution and durable execution matter more than speed. Inside deep mode, the gate opens only for the first question on a thread or a genuinely new topic. One routing table decides this for every turn:

Turn type Plan workflow? First question on a thread Yes New-topic follow-up Yes Entity or metric gap with no safe default No, ask one terminal clarification Source elicitation reply No, re-query only the asking step Extension of the current ask No, retrieve under the locked plan Evidence reply or presentation change No, answer from held evidence or rebuild once

Laziness Protocol. Make the smallest change that solves the problem, and put each repeated choice behind one source of truth. "Does this turn need a plan?" is a choice every code path could make on its own. The routing table makes it once. Reactive mode is the same principle applied to the whole system. Most questions need no plan, so they get none.

Subtract Before You Add. Remove complexity first, then build on the simpler base, with no speculative guards beyond what the requirement needs. Deep mode has four kinds of clarification, and the obvious move is a DeepClarificationMiddleware to own them all. The agent has none. Each kind rides a seam that already exists:

plan-gate clarification   -> submit_plan(clarification=...)
terminal clarification    -> the turn classifier, before any todos exist
source elicitation        -> the source client stamps is_elicitation
"may a report be written?" -> pending_elicitation() in the exit path

Each kind has a different lifetime, so one generic middleware would have had to tell them apart anyway.

Where you build it. Step 8a builds reactive mode. Step 8c builds the turn routing.

docs.title: What are the nouns, and what states can they be in?
docs.text:
You have decided a deep run exists. Before writing logic, name the things it is made of.

The tempting answer. One run record with one UUID, a few booleans (approved, is_running), and a state dict that each node reads and writes as it likes.

What goes wrong. Two bugs in this agent were shape bugs. First, LangGraph state keys default to LastValue, which keeps the old value when a turn does not write the key. A route that wrote only messages left last turn's raw_question in place, and a question about France got an answer about Germany. Second, a crashed worker's replacement re-emitted progress events. The reader deduplicated on the sequence number seq, which takes new values on replay, so every section appeared twice.

The decision. List the nouns, and give each one its own identity and lifecycle:

thread    thread_id                  the conversation, stable forever
turn      cycle                      the question number inside a thread
plan      plan_id = plan-{thread}-{cycle}   stable across replay and refinement
pause     interrupt_id               new for every interrupt
attempt   run_id                     new for every execution attempt
event     idem_key = {task_id}#{n}   stable; seq only orders
tenure    claim_token                new for every lock acquisition
fact      provenance_id              {source}:{plan_id}:{step_id}:{hash}

Give every state key an explicit merge rule. Give the plan a state machine, and let code own its transitions.

Foundational Thinking. Get the data shapes right before writing logic, trace every access pattern, and ask what concurrent actors share. The state schema is where this happens:

class DeepState(TypedDict):
    raw_question: NotRequired[str]                               # LastValue: replace
    messages: Annotated[list[AnyMessage], add_messages]          # reducer: append
    source_results: Annotated[list[SourceResult], operator.add]  # reducer: append
    step_status: Annotated[dict[str, str], operator.or_]         # reducer: merge

step_status is a merge because parallel branches update different plan steps in the same superstep. A LastValue there would let one branch erase another's status. That is the concurrency question asked at the schema, before any branch exists.

Model the Domain. Encode the domain in a structure, such as a state machine, a typed model, or a lookup table, instead of scattered conditionals. The plan lifecycle is a state machine in code:

DRAFT --refine--> DRAFT (modification_count + 1)
DRAFT --approve--> LOCKED --> EXECUTING --> COMPLETE

The model writes plan content only in DRAFT. The locked transition happens in code, on approve, through model_copy. No prompt sentence says "only proceed if the plan is approved", because no branch anywhere needs to check.

Type System Discipline. Make illegal states unrepresentable, and parse external data into typed models at the boundary. Model output is external data. The agent writes plain todos, and project_plan parses them into a typed Plan every time one is needed. A malformed routing tag fails soft. The raw text stays visible in the step title and the routing field is left unset. The model can write inconsistent todos, but it cannot produce an invalid Plan. The cost of skipping this showed up in Capstone 1's Bug 9. An explicit reset [] passed through values.get("entity_groups") or None, became None, was skipped on write, and the next read rehydrated an older turn's entities. Empty and absent were different states, and the coercion merged them.

Not in this agent yet: branded identifiers. Every id above is a plain str, so nothing stops a caller from passing a run_id where a thread_id belongs. A sketch of the fix:

ThreadId = NewType("ThreadId", str)
RunId = NewType("RunId", str)

def enqueue_deep_run(thread_id: ThreadId, run_id: RunId) -> None: ...

With these types, the type checker rejects a swapped call before it runs.

Where you build it. Step 1 builds the state channels. Step 4 builds the identifiers. Step 3 builds the plan state machine.

docs.title: Where are the boundaries, and who may write what?
docs.text:
You have the nouns. Now decide where outside data enters, and which rules the model may break.

The tempting answer. Put the user's defaults in the system prompt. Write the rules there too: "Do not use the spawn_subagent tool." "Only retrieve after the plan is approved."

What goes wrong. Three things broke. The middleware injected "default country: Australia" above a message that said "Actually, give me sales for France", and the injected default won. Some text inside the trusted context block came from conversation summaries, and if it ever contained the literal [/User context], it would close the block early, so whatever followed would read as the user's own instruction. And the framework's built-in sub-agent tool stayed visible to the model, which sometimes called it anyway. A sub-agent runs its retrievals outside the approval gate.

The decision. Inject request-only context in middleware just before each model call. Label it, escape its delimiter, and keep it out of the checkpoint. Split every rule with one test. If code can enforce the rule deterministically, code enforces it and the prompt spends no tokens on it. Tools, the gate, plan status, owner checks and concurrency go to code. The prompt shapes judgment: reasoning order, the priority of explicit entities over defaults, and grounding.

Boundary Discipline. Validate and handle errors at system boundaries, trust typed data inside, and keep business logic in pure functions. Prompt assembly is a pure function, structured state in and a string out, with the guard at the exact point where untrusted text crosses in:

def compose_with_context(content: str, context: str) -> str:
    safe_context = context.replace("[/User context]", "[/user context]")
    return f"[User context]\n{safe_context}\n[/User context]\n\n{content}"

Because it is pure, you can test it without a model. The approve endpoint follows the same rule. It checks owner_id, plan_id and interrupt_id once, at the HTTP boundary, and the code after that trusts the result.

Encode Lessons in Structure. When you find yourself writing the same instruction a second time, encode it as a check or as code. If the fix is structural, use only the structural fix. The tool rule became a middleware that removes tools from the request:

class AllowedToolsMiddleware(AgentMiddleware):
    def _filter(self, request):
        tools = [t for t in request.tools if t.name in self._allowed]
        return request.override(tools=tools)   # the model never sees the rest

The prompt does not also say "don't call spawn_subagent." That sentence would be the symptom of a fix that is already in place. The same principle shows up outside the prompt. After a per-job asyncio.run() broke a cached HTTP client, a startup guard now turns any reintroduced per-job asyncio.run() into a named error.

Some lessons cannot be encoded. For those, the principle says to make the instruction more prominent and show the failure mode. Grounding is the clearest case. No code can tell whether a sentence came from a tool result or from training data. So the prompt line names every verb the model used to negotiate around it, "Never state, estimate, OR approximate", and it tells the model to mark a failed retrieval as completed, because a "failed" status the status map did not recognize had sent the executor into an endless retry.

Where you build it. Step 2 builds the injection boundary. Step 8 applies the prompt-or-structure test to the whole orchestrator.

docs.title: Where does the human come in, and does anything wait on them?
docs.text:
The requirement says a human approves the plan. Work out exactly where, and what happens while they think.

The tempting answer. Hold the request open while the human reads the plan, then resume when the approval callback arrives. For refinement, loop inside submit_plan and call an LLM to apply the feedback. When the agent is unsure about anything, ask the user.

What goes wrong. Approval can take minutes or days, and no load balancer holds a connection that long. The refine loop needs a second, out-of-band model that does not share the agent's prompt, tools or conversation, so two models end up writing one plan. The browser causes trouble even when nobody is approving anything. It closes the stream the moment it sees the end frame, which cancels any await after that frame, so a turn's save never ran and nothing logged it. And asking too often has its own cost, which you saw in the evaluation tradeoff above.

The decision. interrupt() writes the pause into the checkpoint, and the request ends. Between the plan request and the approve request, nothing is running. Approval is a second request that validates the pause, stages the decision, queues the work, and returns 202 queued. Refine is the agent's own loop. The tool returns the feedback as a ToolMessage, and the agent edits its todos and calls submit_plan again. Progress streams to the browser over SSE. Required writes start before the terminal frame, and the research stream ends when run-state says the run is finished, not when a sentinel event arrives.

Never Block on the Human. The human supervises asynchronously. Proceed on reversible work, present the result, and let the human course-correct, saving confirmation for actions that cannot be undone. This agent applies it at two levels. At the system level, it stops only where the requirement demands, before research that spends real money, and even there no process waits:

POST /chat/stream?mode=deep   -> plan streamed, interrupt() persisted, request ends
   ... minutes or days pass; no process is running ...
POST /deep/{thread_id}/approve/async -> validate, stage decision, queue, 202 queued

At the agent level, it proceeds under a stated assumption instead of opening a separate question round:

Clarification:
  "SOURCE_A and SOURCE_B use different market definitions. I will align on
   retail market unless you refine the plan."

The reactive path has a matching rule. ClarificationGuardMiddleware sees that the previous turn already asked a question, and injects a default-and-declare instruction so the agent never asks twice in a row. The agent asks a terminal question only when a required entity or metric has no safe default.

Experience First. When implementation convenience conflicts with the user's experience, choose the experience. The user includes whoever maintains the code next. The plan card shows "query SOURCE_A for BRAND_A sales by market", not "do research", because a human who cannot evaluate a plan approves it blindly. When one source returns data and another asks back, the message names both facts:

"I have the promotion lift figures. For regional sales, the source asks:
in-store or online?"

The stream ends on durable run-state, so after a worker crash the browser gets a terminal frame with a reason and never spins forever.

Where you build it. Step 3 builds the gate and the 202 path. Step 5 builds streaming that the work outlives. Step 8b builds the four clarification shapes.

docs.title: What happens when it crashes halfway?
docs.text:
The approved run now executes on a background worker for tens of minutes. Assume the worker dies at the worst possible line.

The tempting answer. Catch the exception and retry the run from the start. Delete the queue message as soon as it arrives so nobody else picks it up. Deduplicate feed lines by their sequence number.

What goes wrong. SQS delivers at least once, and LangGraph re-runs an interrupted node from its beginning. A Slack notification placed before interrupt() fires once on the proposal and once more on every resume. A replayed node re-emits its feed lines with new seq values, so a seq-based reader shows them twice. A message deleted on receive is gone when the worker dies, and the approved run never happens.

The decision. Every step reads durable state and applies only the difference. The approve path writes in a fixed order. Workers delete the queue message last. Every identity that has to be recognized after a crash is derived from position, not from a counter or the clock.

Make Operations Idempotent. Design each operation to converge on the same end state no matter how many times it runs or where the previous run stopped. Ask "what if this runs twice?" and "what if the last run crashed at every possible point?" The approve path answers both through its write order:

checkpoint resume decision -> run-state queued -> queue message

A lost message can be re-sent. A lost approval cannot be rebuilt. The feed answers the same questions with two values that behave in opposite ways on replay:

Attempt 1   seq 3  taskB#0  Querying ONLINE...
            seq 4  taskB#1  ONLINE 88 rows        <- crash before commit
Attempt 2   seq 5  taskB#0  Querying ONLINE...    <- new seq, same idem_key: skipped
            seq 6  taskB#1  ONLINE 88 rows        <- new seq, same idem_key: skipped
            seq 7  taskC#0  Report ready          <- shown

The report gets the same treatment. cycle_stamp = {plan_id, sorted provenance_ids} is stored as reported_cycle, so a redelivery that reaches the exit path with the same evidence set writes nothing. The principle also says anything a run leaves behind must be recognizable as stale by the next run. A lock left by a crashed worker carries expires_at, and the acquire condition compares it against the current time. DynamoDB's ttl sweeper can run hours late, so no lock logic depends on it.

Where you build it. Step 7 builds the worker ritual and the write order. Step 7a builds the replay-stable feed. Step 4 explains which ids must stay stable on replay.

docs.title: What happens when two things happen at once?
docs.text:
Crashes are one source of repeated work. Concurrency is the other. A user double-clicks Approve, and two API replicas receive the clicks fifty milliseconds apart.

The tempting answer. Add a threading.Lock around the resume. Or, to be safe, one global lock around all runs. Store everything in one table so it is all in one place.

What goes wrong. A threading.Lock lives in one replica's memory, and the other replica cannot see it. Both resumes run, the plan executes twice, and the checkpoint keeps whichever finished last. A global lock serializes threads that never touch each other. One table for checkpoints and feed lines means a feed write failure can take down a real run.

The decision. First remove the sharing. Different threads share nothing, so they run fully in parallel. Truth and narration go in separate tables. Each thread's lock lives under its own partition key. Then, where one writer really is required, serialize structurally. LangGraph does not support two runs on one thread, so that invariant gets a FIFO message group, a conditional-write claim with a tenure token, and a write fence on the data itself.

Separate Before Serializing Shared State. When concurrent actors might write the same object, first ask whether they need the same object, and give each its own if not. Serialize structurally only when one shared writer is a real invariant. The separation shows up in the table layout:

Table Item PK Owner {env}-agent-checkpoints checkpoint LangGraph's own scheme the saver {env}-agent-checkpoints resume claim CLAIM#{thread_id} the API, one approve at a time {env}-agent-events feed line {thread_id}, SK seq the worker's emitter {env}-agent-events run lock lock#{thread_id} the worker, one per thread

Every lock has its own partition, so there is no hot lock row. An outage of the events table quiets the feed while the run keeps executing. The reader's dedup set lives per connection in API memory, so the durable log never has to track what each user has seen. Where serialization is real, it lives in the transport and the data, not in a convention:

sqs.send_message(QueueUrl=queue_url, MessageBody=body, MessageGroupId=thread_id)

table.put_item(
    Item={"PK": f"CLAIM#{thread_id}", "SK": "RESUME", "claim_token": token, "expires_at": now + 1800},
    ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(PK) OR expires_at < :now",
    ExpressionAttributeValues={":now": now},
)

The second click's write fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException, and the API returns 409. Every renew and release is conditional on claim_token, so a frozen worker that wakes up after losing its lease cannot delete the new holder's claim. Capstone 1's Bug 8 was the version that released unconditionally.

Where you build it. The DynamoDB and SQS bridge teaches the two primitives. Step 6 builds the claim, the lease and the fence. Step 7 builds the two tables and the per-thread group.

docs.title: How much should the model see?
docs.text:
The run is durable and serialized. Now look at it from the model's side. A user asks "and how does that compare to last quarter?", and the sales it needs were pulled two turns ago.

The tempting answer. Paste the prior results back into the context so the model can reuse them. Or give it a search_held_data tool to look them up.

What goes wrong. One retrieval can be thousands of rows, and a long thread holds megabytes. Pasting them back buries the conversation, uses up the token budget, and drowns the one line that matters. The lookup tool fails without any signal. When the model does not think to call it, it re-queries, and nothing records the missed reuse. Reuse can also turn into invention, when the model derives new figures from a fading memory of old ones.

The decision. Show the model an index, never a copy. DataManifestMiddleware rebuilds a [held data] block on every model call. Each result gets one line of about 100 bytes, showing the newest 30, newest first, with one rollup line for the rest. Reuse is a plan step the human can see, and it may reuse prose but never numbers.

Guard the Context Window. A full context window degrades reasoning, so keep summaries in the working context and route bulk payloads somewhere else. Here the bulk payloads stay in state["source_results"], and the model sees this:

[held data] - results already retrieved this thread. Prefer reusing a held result
over re-querying; check `retrieved` for staleness. Reference results by provenance id.
- REGIONAL:plan-chat-1-1:step-1:a3f9c2d1 | ok=True | rows=412 | retrieved 2026-09-10 | NZ sales by region, 2024
...plus 3 older result(s) held in state - ask the user before assuming their content.
[/held data]

rows=412 tells the model that data exists to fetch by name. It does not put the rows in the window. The cap is 30 lines because attention is the limit, not tokens. The same principle sets the loop bound. RetrievalBudgetMiddleware caps a plan cycle at six retrieval rounds, and a turn that queries three sources in parallel spends one round.

Where you build it. Step 8d builds the manifest and the reuse rules.

docs.title: How will the next engineer find their way around the code?
docs.text:
The design now has gates, middlewares, workers, locks and a feed. Picture the engineer who opens it six months from now because a report came back about the wrong country.

The tempting answer. Put it all in one agent.py. Or split it by phase into load, plan, execute and save.

What goes wrong. Capstone 1's Bug 5 was an invariant spread across three files with no owner. Starting a turn meant writing three LastValue channels together. The hand-built dict lived in one file, the channel declarations in another, and the readers in a third. A caller that wrote only messages silently kept the previous turn's context. Phase-named modules make this worse, because the same domain rule gets repeated at every phase.

The decision. Group modules by the boundary they own, so every silent failure has one obvious first file. Declare each state channel next to its only writer. Keep shared names in one contract module.

Minimize Reader Load. Count the layers between a reader's question and its answer and the hidden state they must hold in their head, then cut both. The test is whether a new reader can answer "where does X come from?" in under thirty seconds. For raw_question, the answer is one file:

# proposal_context.py
class _UserContextState(AgentState):
    raw_question: NotRequired[str]
    user_context: NotRequired[str]

def build_proposal_graph_input(question: str, user_context: str) -> dict: ...

The channel declaration, the one writer, and the middleware that reads it sit together. LangGraph merges this schema with DeepState in gate.py at compile time, so co-location costs nothing at runtime. The package map then works as a review index:

If the bug is about... Look first in... A plan approved, refined or locked incorrectly gate.py, plan.py A stale default changed model behavior proposal_context.py, manifest.py A run executed twice or did not resume resume_claim.py, resume_decision.py, run_queue.py, worker_lock.py Progress duplicated or disappeared curator.py, event_log.py

Where you build it. Step 8e maps every module group.

docs.title: In what order do I build it so each piece proves itself?
docs.text:
You know what to build. The last design question before you start is the order.

The tempting answer. Build the whole graph, wire in the queue and the worker, then test end to end once everything exists.

What goes wrong. Step 3 names its hardest unit, adding plan_id and interrupt_id validation, because that is where idempotency and stale-state bugs both surface. If the queue, the worker and the lock are already stacked on top when that first goes red, you cannot tell which layer broke.

The decision. Build in units that each end in a check you can run. Write the check as a script or test that anyone can rerun, not as a one-time manual try.

Sequence work into verifiable units. Break the work into small units that each end in a state you can check, and do not start the next one until the current one is green. Step 3 lays out its own build this way:

1. Plan generation only. No interrupt. Validate content.
2. Add interrupt(). Resume from a test with Command(resume={"type": "approve"}).
3. Add the approve endpoint. Two real requests.
4. Add the refine path. Feedback returns as a ToolMessage.
5. Add plan_id and interrupt_id validation. Test the stale-tab case.
6. Add the async approve path. Stage, write queued, enqueue, return 202.
7. Add the claim. Two simultaneous approves give one run and one conflict.

The series runs in the same order. State comes before context, and context before approval. Identifiers come after you have seen a plan pause and resume. Locks come after the browser can double-click Approve. Prompt design comes after code already owns the boundaries.

Build the Lever. For any non-trivial work, build the tool that does or proves it, such as a script or a rerunnable check, so a reviewer can rerun it instead of trusting you. Each unit here has a lever. Step 5's lever is a forced-disconnect test that closes the client right after the first terminal frame and asserts that the save still completes. Step 6's is a takeover scenario. A acquires, A's lease expires, B acquires, A tries to release, and B's claim must remain. For the model's behavior, the lever is the evaluation loop, with a versioned dataset, a code grader where the check can be stated exactly, and per-case verdicts:

def grade_sources(case, run) -> str:
    return "correct" if run.sources_called == case["expected_sources"] else "incorrect"

Its sixth rule turns every production failure into a case before the fix lands, so the dataset grows wherever the agent has actually failed.

Where you build it. Step 3 gives the unit sequence for the gate. The evaluation bridge gives the evaluation loop.

docs.title: When it breaks, how do I fix it for real?
docs.text:
It will break anyway. Before one release, code review found nine bugs in this agent, and none of them crashed.

The tempting answer. Patch the line where the symptom showed up. If a scan finds the wrong record, make the scan smarter. If the model uses a stale default, stop injecting the default in that phase.

What goes wrong. Capstone 1's Bug 1 is the clearest case. During execution, middleware injected "default country: Australia" on every model call, including calls after the human had approved a plan for Germany. The fresh default sat near the top of the prompt, the approval sat lower in history, and the report came back about Australia. The obvious fix was to gate injection on plan["status"] == "locked". That fix broke multi-turn sessions.

The decision. Trace each symptom to the first wrong decision. When a fix fails, write down what it assumed before trying another.

Fix Root Causes. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system did something wrong and fix it there. A guard counts as a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate. Bug 9 shows the trace. Its symptom was a follow-up planned against an older topic's entities. The cause went three levels deep:

entity_groups = values.get("entity_groups") or None   # [] reset becomes None
if md.entity_groups: item["entity_groups"] = ...       # None is not written
for msg in reversed(memory): if groups: return groups  # scan lands on an older turn

Patching the scan would hide the bug. The first wrong decision was storing session state inside message records, so the fix moved it to a purpose-built store with direct overwrite, where [] means reset and None means never set. Bug 3 shows the guard rule from the other side. A multimodal message with list content is a legitimate state, so the code that broke on it, a backward scan that silently retargeted an older message, was the root cause. The fix stops and logs at that point. The principle also says to check for the pattern, not just the instance. In Bug 7, quick mode had already handled a missing chat_id correctly by skipping the write.

Attack the Premise. When fixes that share one premise keep failing the same check, write the premise down and test it directly before writing another fix that assumes it. The plan-status gate rested on one sentence:

Premise: the plan channel tells a model call which phase it belongs to.
Test:    turn 2 asks a new question on the same thread.
         The plan channel still holds turn 1's LOCKED plan.
         Turn 2 is planning, but the gate reads "locked" and drops the defaults it needs.
Result:  premise false. plan is a sticky LastValue channel, and phase is not stored in it.

The series records one failed fix here, and the principle's trigger is two. Writing the premise down after the first failure was cheaper than a second fix built on the same belief. With the premise gone, code had no reliable phase signal. The rule moved into the context block, which the model reads alongside the conversation that shows the approval:

"[User context - entities named explicitly in the question always win over these defaults, "
"and once a research plan is approved and locked, the locked plan's entities "
"win over these defaults]\n"

Where you build it. Capstone 1 walks through all nine bugs. Step 8 steps through Bug 1.

docs.title: When the requirements change, what do I do with the design I already have?
docs.text:
The last question is about time. Requirements arrive after code exists. In this agent the biggest one was human approval before anything expensive runs.

The tempting answer. Bolt it on. Chapter 1's exercise puts it in a colleague's words: "Easy, just interrupt the function, wait for the approval callback, then resume." Later, once approval works, keep the approve request streaming execution back to the browser, because that is convenient for local testing.

What goes wrong. The bolted-on version holds a connection open for days. The streaming approve request ties a forty-minute run to one HTTP response and one API process, so a closed laptop or a deploy kills research the human already approved.

The decision. Treat approval as a requirement that was there from the start, which changes the topology. Then converge on the target, an approve that returns 202 queued and a worker that resumes with None, rather than maintaining both paths. Before committing to an unfamiliar design, compare real alternatives.

Redesign From First Principles. When a new requirement arrives, do not bolt it on. Ask what you would build if it had been a foundational assumption, and carry the change through every reference. With approval assumed from day one, a turn spans several HTTP requests. That needs durable checkpointed state that any replica can load, a pause that serializes to storage instead of blocking a thread (interrupt()), and a separate endpoint that delivers the decision. It also changed the payload, which now carries plan_id, interrupt_id and owner_id so the second request can prove it is approving the pause the human saw.

Outcome-Oriented Execution. In a planned rewrite, converge on the verified end state instead of keeping intermediate states smooth with throwaway compatibility code. The synchronous approve stream helped with local testing, but it was never the production target. The series teaches only the target path, and the learning record states the rule directly:

approval writes the resume decision into the checkpoint, writes run-state as queued,
enqueues SQS FIFO, and returns 202 queued; a worker later resumes with None.
The older synchronous approval stream is only a legacy/interim path.

Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs. When a new internal API replaces an old one, migrate every caller and delete the old API in the same wave, and update the tests to assert the new contract. The factory from Bug 5 is the small example. Once build_proposal_graph_input existed, every route that started the graph moved onto it, and the hand-built dicts went away, so a forgotten key could no longer happen. For the synchronous approve stream, the series records that it is legacy but not when it was deleted. The principle says when. Delete it in the same change that moves its last caller and its tests onto the 202 path, so nobody new copies the old shape.

Exhaust the Design Space. For a decision with no precedent, build two or three competing designs and compare them side by side before you commit. Context injection was that kind of decision, and four designs were compared:

system prompt injection     rejected: the orchestrator prompt is request-invariant and cached
checkpointed message        rejected: the block would pile up in history across turns
tool call                   rejected: an extra round trip, and the model can skip it
middleware before the call  chosen:   injected after the checkpoint is read, never stored

The data manifest went through the same comparison, an ambient index against a search_held_data tool, and the tool lost because it fails without a signal. Bug 1's fix was a third comparison, a code gate against a prompt rule, and the prompt rule won only after the code gate's premise failed.

Where you build it. Step 3 builds the gate that approval requires. Chapter 3 shows the async approve path end to end. Capstone 1 records the four injection designs.

docs.title: From answers to architecture
docs.text:
Put the twelve answers next to each other and the system takes shape. Durable state and explicit identities give you a checkpoint that any process can reload. The human's pause is a record in that checkpoint, so approval becomes a second request that stages a decision and queues a pointer. A per-thread queue group and a fenced claim give each thread one writer. Truth and narration need separate homes, so the worker writes curated events to their own table and the browser tails them. Chapter 3 draws that system end to end, with the four durable records, the order approval writes them, and the worker that resumes with no input. Read it as the architecture these answers produce.

You should now understand

  • The twelve design questions, and why they come in this order
  • The tempting first answer to each, and the real bug it caused in this agent
  • Which principle settles each question, and the code or state trace that shows it
  • Which Step builds each answer
Try this

A teammate proposes adding a line to the orchestrator prompt: "Never call query_market_data before the plan is approved." Which design question does this belong to, and what do you tell them?

Answer

It belongs to the boundaries question. Code can enforce this rule deterministically, so it belongs in structure, not in the prompt. The gate's interrupt() already stops execution until the human resumes, and AllowedToolsMiddleware controls which tools the model can see. A prompt sentence would compete with the model's other instincts and sometimes lose. Encode Lessons in Structure also says that once the structural fix exists, you do not repeat it as text.

Next: Chapter 3 · End-to-end architecture and orchestrator flow. The architecture these answers produce, traced from the first question to the worker's last write.

docs.title: Chapter 3 · End-to-end architecture and orchestrator flow
docs.text:
Before building state, prompts, queues, or locks one at a time, hold the whole run in your head.

This chapter is a map, not a lesson, and it moves fast. Hold onto three things: the four durable records and their jobs, the order in which approval writes them, and why the worker resumes from the checkpoint with no input. Everything else here, such as pending writes, SQS, DynamoDB and the event curator, is fine to skim now. Steps 1 to 7 build each piece, and the terms list at the end of Chapter 1 gives a sentence on each word.

A production deep agent is a handoff chain across several requests and processes:

API plans -> checkpoint pauses -> human approves -> API queues -> worker resumes -> SSE tails events

Each arrow crosses a seam where a silent failure can enter. This chapter gives you the map so the implementation chapters have somewhere to attach.

docs.title: The four durable records
docs.text:
One approved research turn has four different records, with four different jobs:

Record Job Who reads it Checkpoint Graph truth: state, pending interrupt, pending resume decision LangGraph and approval validation Run-state Durable lifecycle: queued, running, retrying, completed, failed API, worker, SSE tail, failure detector Queue message A tiny pointer: thread_id, run_id Worker Event log Curated progress feed for humans Browser SSE tail

The checkpoint is the graph's source of truth. The event log is narration. The queue is only a pointer. Run-state is the lifecycle marker that lets the UI stop waiting when work completed or failed.

If you blur these together, the system becomes hard to repair after a crash. A lost event should not lose the run. A lost queue message should be re-enqueueable. A completed worker should not need a live browser to make completion true.

The code mirrors these records, with one module group per boundary. Step 8e maps every module once you have seen what each boundary does.

docs.title: Phase 1: planning runs in the API
docs.text:
The first request starts from a user question.

POST /chat/stream?mode=deep
  -> build graph input for this turn
  -> inject user context at model-call time
  -> orchestrator writes todos
  -> submit_plan projects a typed plan
  -> interrupt() persists the pause
  -> API streams a plan event and closes at interrupt

The plan phase is allowed to be synchronous because it ends quickly at the gate. The browser watches it over SSE, but the artifact that matters is the checkpoint, which now contains state plus a pending interrupt payload.

The submit_plan tool is deliberately split by concern:

  • The plan's step structure is derived from the agent's write_todos state.
  • The resolved entities arrive as an explicit entities tool argument.
  • The gate sanitizes those entities and persists them to state["entity_groups"].

The model authors the raw planning intent. Code projects and sanitizes the approved shape.

docs.title: Phase 2: approval stages intent, then queues work
docs.text:
In the production path, the approval request does not run research.

POST /deep/{thread_id}/approve/async
  -> read pending interrupt from checkpoint
  -> validate owner, plan, and interrupt
  -> saver.put_writes((RESUME, {"type": "approve"}), task=NULL_TASK_ID)
  -> put run-state: status = queued
  -> enqueue SQS FIFO message, MessageGroupId = thread_id
  -> return 202 queued

The resume decision is a LangGraph pending write placed in the checkpoint's resume slot so the paused interrupt() can consume it later. It is not a normal state field, so neither LastValue nor a reducer applies.

The write order is the contract:

checkpoint resume decision -> run-state queued -> queue message

A queue message can be re-sent. A human approval decision cannot be reconstructed safely after the fact, so it is written first.

An earlier design had the approve request itself stream execution synchronously in the HTTP response. That helped with local testing but was never the production target. The production path returns 202 queued and lets a separate background worker own the long run.

docs.title: Phase 3: the worker resumes with no input
docs.text:
When the worker receives the FIFO message, it already has everything it needs.

SQS receive
  -> stamp attempt/receive count into run-state
  -> acquire lock#{thread_id}
  -> compile graph with a lease-extending saver
  -> agent.astream_events(None, config)
  -> curate raw events into StreamEnvelope
  -> write terminal run-state
  -> release lock
  -> delete SQS message last

The None is deliberate. Approval was already staged in the checkpoint as a pending resume write, so LangGraph reloads the checkpoint, re-enters the paused interrupt(), drains the pending resume value, and continues.

Deleting the SQS message is last because loss is worse than duplication. If the worker crashes before terminal status, the message redelivers and another worker resumes from the checkpoint.

docs.title: Phase 4: the browser tails a projection
docs.text:
The frontend should never consume raw LangGraph or DeepAgents events. Those are framework internals. The UI gets a curated StreamEnvelope.

The two phases use different streaming paths:

PLAN PHASE
──────────
  Browser ←── SSE ←── API (curator runs here, inline)

RESEARCH PHASE
──────────────
  Worker (curator runs here)
      │
      │  writes curated events
      ▼
  DynamoDB event log
  (one row per event, keyed by thread_id + seq)
      │
      │  browser polls: "give me rows where seq > my Last-Event-ID"
      ▼
  API SSE tail endpoint
      │
      ▼
  Browser

During research, the API and the worker never talk to each other directly. The worker writes to the event log. The API reads from it. The browser's Last-Event-ID header is the cursor. If the browser reconnects after a network blip, it sends the last seq it saw, and the API picks up from there. No events are lost.

Termination is status-based, not sentinel-based:

Browser asks: "are we done?"
API checks: run-state record in database

  if status == "running"  → keep tailing the event log
  if status == "completed"  → send terminal frame, close stream
  if status == "failed"     → send terminal frame, close stream

if run.status in ("completed", "failed"):
    yield terminal_frame(run.status)
    return

Do not rely only on a final done event. A crash can skip a sentinel. A run-state record can still be flipped to failed by a worker, redelivery path, or detector, letting the browser stop with a visible reason.

docs.title: The orchestrator's real tool surface
docs.text:
The public lessons sometimes use query_source as a teaching simplification. In production, the orchestrator had seven allowed tools:

write_todos
submit_plan
query_cortex
query_market_data
run_analysis
rebuild_artifacts
read_file

The allow-list enforces the boundary. Only plan-safe planning tools are reachable before approval, and only plan-gated retrieval or synthesis tools are reachable after approval. Sub-agent tools are not directly reachable by the orchestrator.

docs.title: The whole run
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant A as API
    participant C as Checkpoint
    participant R as Run-state
    participant Q as SQS FIFO
    participant W as Worker
    participant E as Event log

    B->>A: Ask deep question
    A->>C: Run plan phase and interrupt
    A-->>B: SSE plan + interrupt
    B->>A: Approve interrupt_id
    A->>C: Stage pending resume decision
    A->>R: status = queued
    A->>Q: enqueue {thread_id, run_id}
    A-->>B: 202 queued
    W->>Q: receive message
    W->>R: status = running/retrying
    W->>C: resume with None
    W->>E: write curated events
    B->>A: Open research SSE
    A->>E: tail from Last-Event-ID
    A-->>B: StreamEnvelope events
    W->>R: status = completed/failed
    W->>Q: delete message last

The rest of the series now zooms into each box: state, context, approval, identifiers, streams, locks, queue execution, prompt design, and the failure modes that happen when any seam lies.

You should now understand

  • Why production approval queues work instead of streaming execution inside the approval request
  • Why the resume decision lives in checkpoint pending writes, not in ordinary state
  • Why the worker resumes with None
  • Why checkpoints, run-state, queue messages, and event logs are separate records
  • Why raw framework events are curated before the frontend sees them
Try this

The approval endpoint has validated the pending interrupt. Should it call the graph with Command(resume={"type": "approve"}) and stream research work to the browser, or should it write the resume decision, queue the run, and return?

Answer

In the production path, it writes the resume decision into the checkpoint, writes run-state as queued, enqueues the FIFO message, and returns 202 queued. A worker later resumes the graph with None because the decision is already staged in the checkpoint.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Every term the series uses, defined once. Each article links here the first time it uses one of these words. If a passage ever loses you, this is the page to keep open beside it.

The definitions are ordered roughly from "things a normal web engineer already knows" to "things specific to agent systems."

docs.title: Replica
docs.text: One of several identical copies of your API server running at once, behind a load balancer. Two requests from the same user can land on two different replicas. Anything one replica keeps in its own memory is invisible to the others. That is why shared state has to live in a database, not in a Python variable.

docs.title: SSE (Server-Sent Events)
docs.text: A long-lived HTTP response where the server keeps sending small text frames over time instead of one final body. It is how an agent streams progress ("planning…", "querying…") to a browser. The browser's built-in EventSource object consumes it. See Step 5 · Streaming and background work.

docs.title: Last-Event-ID
docs.text: A header the browser's EventSource automatically re-sends when it reconnects after a dropped connection. It contains the id: of the last frame the browser received. The server uses it as a cursor to resume the stream exactly where it left off.

docs.title: FIFO queue
docs.text: A "first-in, first-out" message queue. Messages are delivered in order. The variant used here also guarantees that only one message per group is being processed at a time. That is how "one worker per conversation" becomes a property of the queue instead of code you write.

docs.title: Visibility timeout
docs.text: When a worker picks up a queue message, the queue hides it from other workers for a set time. If the worker finishes and deletes the message, it is gone. If the worker dies and the timeout lapses, the queue makes the message visible again and another worker gets it. This is the mechanism that redelivers work after a crash.

docs.title: DLQ (dead-letter queue)
docs.text: A separate queue where a message lands after it has failed too many times ("poison pill"). Instead of retrying forever, the system parks it here and raises an alarm so a human can look. In this design it is the only thing that pages a person.

docs.title: TTL (time-to-live)
docs.text: An expiry timestamp on a database row. A background sweeper deletes rows past their TTL, eventually. It is janitorial cleanup, not a precise timer. Deletion can lag by hours, so correctness must never depend on it.

docs.title: Conditional write
docs.text: A database write that only succeeds if a condition is true at the moment of writing. The check and the write happen together, atomically, with no gap for a second writer to sneak in. It is the most important primitive in the series, because it picks one winner out of a race.

docs.title: attribute_not_exists(PK)
docs.text: The condition "only write this if there is no item with this primary key yet." In plain English: "only if this slot is empty." For a lock it means "acquire only if nobody holds it." See Step 6 · Distributed locks.

docs.title: ConditionExpression
docs.text: The DynamoDB parameter that carries a conditional write's condition. When the condition is false, DynamoDB rejects the write with a ConditionalCheckFailedException, which your code treats as the normal "someone else got there first" signal, not an error.

docs.title: PK / SK
docs.text: Partition key and sort key: the two parts of a DynamoDB item's address. PK groups related items together; SK orders them within the group. One table can hold several kinds of item by giving them different PK prefixes (for example run#abc vs lock#abc).

docs.title: Lock
docs.text: A rule enforced through data: "only one process may act on X at a time." Here a lock is not a language primitive; it is a row in a database that every replica can see.

docs.title: Claim
docs.text: This series' word for a lock used to guard a resumable run. Before running, a request writes a small marker (the claim) that says "I am running this thread; hands off." If the marker already exists and is still live, another request got there first. Same idea as a lock, named for what it does.

docs.title: Lease
docs.text: The claim's expiry. A claim is deliberately short-lived so that if its holder crashes, the thread is not wedged forever. A healthy holder keeps pushing the expiry forward while it works ("renewing the lease"). See Step 6 · Distributed locks.

docs.title: Token (ownership token / claim_token)
docs.text: A fresh random string minted each time a claim is acquired. It identifies this specific tenure, not the worker. Every write to the claim is guarded by "only if the stored token still equals mine," so a process that lost the claim can neither renew nor delete it. Think of a hotel key card: reprogramming the door for a new guest silently invalidates the old card.

docs.title: Fencing / write fence
docs.text: A backstop for when even a lock check races. Every real data write is made conditional on a slot only the rightful owner can fill. A stale process ("zombie") collides on its very next write, so the corruption attempt is itself the detection. See Step 6 · Distributed locks.

docs.title: Zombie
docs.text: A worker that froze (a long pause, a network partition) without dying, lost its claim to a replacement, then woke up still believing it owns the thread. The write fence exists to catch it.

docs.title: LangGraph terms
docs.text: LangGraph is the framework that runs the agent as a graph of steps. These terms are how it models a run.

docs.title: Node
docs.text: One step in the graph: a function that reads the current state and returns an update to it. An agent's "call the model" and "run a tool" are nodes.

docs.title: State
docs.text: The dictionary the graph reads and writes as it runs. It holds named channels like messages, plan, and raw_question. See Step 1 · State and checkpoints.

docs.title: Channel
docs.text: One key in the state, with a rule for what happens when a node writes it. The two rules that matter: LastValue (a new write replaces the old value) and reducer (a new write combines with the old value, e.g. appending to a message list).

docs.title: LastValue (the footgun)
docs.text: The default channel rule: the latest write wins. The trap: not writing a key does not clear it; it keeps whatever the last checkpoint held. So a new turn that forgets to overwrite a channel silently inherits the previous turn's value.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: The saved copy of the graph's state at a point in time, plus LangGraph's bookkeeping. It lives in a database, so a later HTTP request, even on a different replica, can reload it and continue. It is the run's source of truth.

docs.title: Checkpointer / saver
docs.text: The component that writes checkpoints. In this series it writes to DynamoDB. You rarely call it directly; LangGraph calls it automatically after each step.

docs.title: Super-step
docs.text: One "tick" of the graph: the batch of nodes that run together before the next checkpoint is written. Checkpoints happen per super-step.

docs.title: interrupt()
docs.text: The one primitive for pausing a graph to wait for a human. It saves state to the checkpoint and raises a special exception; the HTTP response returns with whatever streamed so far, and the graph freezes in the database. See Step 3 · Planning and human approval.

docs.title: Resume / Command(resume=…)
docs.text: Continuing a paused graph. A later HTTP request sends Command(resume=value); LangGraph reloads the checkpoint and delivers value as the return of the original interrupt() call. Resume re-runs the current node from the top, so everything before interrupt() runs again on every resume.

docs.title: Pending resume write
docs.text: The low-level checkpoint entry that carries a human decision back into a paused interrupt(). In the production approve path, the API stages (RESUME, {"type": "approve"}) with saver.put_writes() before enqueueing work. This is not a normal state channel: it is neither LastValue nor a reducer, and it does not appear in get_state().values.

docs.title: Thread / thread_id
docs.text: The durable identity of one conversation or run. Same thread_id means same graph thread and same checkpoint. Refine and approve requests, possibly minutes apart on different replicas, find each other by sharing a thread_id.

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text: Code that wraps a model call to change the request just before it reaches the model, without touching saved state. Used here to inject per-user context into the prompt, and to hide tools the agent is not allowed to use.

docs.title: ToolMessage
docs.text: The result of a tool call, fed back to the model as its next input. This series uses it as a continuation signal: after a human approves or refines, the gate returns a ToolMessage telling the model what to do next, because a tool result has higher salience than the system prompt.

docs.title: Deep agent
docs.text: An agent that drafts a multi-step plan, pauses for a human to approve it, then executes it over many tool calls, possibly for tens of minutes. Its state lives in a checkpoint store rather than in one process, so a different request or worker can pick the run up. Contrast reactive mode, which answers in one pass. See Chapter 1 · Problem, design, and implementation plan and Step 8a · Reactive mode and its prompt.

docs.title: Worker
docs.text: A background process that receives an approved run from the queue and executes it. It is separate from the API process that took the user's request, so it can run on another machine, survive a deploy, or be replaced by a second worker after a crash. See Step 7 · Queue and worker execution.

docs.title: Gate
docs.text: The approval checkpoint in the workflow, implemented as the submit_plan tool. It projects the plan, calls interrupt() once, and returns an instruction. See Step 3 · Planning and human approval.

docs.title: Plan / plan_id / interrupt_id
docs.text: The plan is the set of research steps the human approves. plan_id is stable across refinements (it identifies the plan, not the revision). interrupt_id is minted fresh on every pause, so it identifies the exact revision the user was looking at. That is what catches a stale browser tab approving an out-of-date plan.

docs.title: Projection
docs.text: A value derived from a source of truth, rebuilt on demand rather than stored and mutated. The typed Plan is a projection over the agent's raw todo list; the user-facing event feed is a projection over the run's real state. A projection can be thrown away and recomputed, which is what makes the system's persistence safe.

docs.title: Run-state
docs.text: A single database row that tracks the lifecycle of one run attempt. Fields: thread_id, run_id, status, receive_count, and optionally a reason on failure. Status moves through: queued (written by the API on approval) → running / retrying (written by the worker on pickup) → completed / failed (written last). The SSE tail polls this record to decide when to close the browser stream. It must not rely only on a final stream sentinel, because a crashed worker may never write one.

docs.title: StreamEnvelope
docs.text: The curated event shape the frontend receives. Raw LangGraph or DeepAgents events are framework internals; the API or worker projects them into StreamEnvelope records before the UI sees them.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: The property that doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once. Critical wherever work can be retried or replayed after a crash.

docs.title: Idempotency key
docs.text: A value that identifies a logical event regardless of which attempt produced it. Because it is derived from execution position (not from a counter or a random id), a replayed event carries the same key and the reader can dedupe it. See Step 7a · The event feed and idempotency.

docs.title: Sequence number (seq)
docs.text: A plain counter that gives the event feed a total order and doubles as the reader's cursor. Unlike the idempotency key, it takes new values on replay, which is why the two are kept separate.

docs.title: Heartbeat
docs.text: A periodic "I am still alive" signal. Here it is tied to progress (each checkpoint write) rather than a wall-clock timer, so a process that is alive-but-stuck stops beating and gets reclaimed. See Step 7 · Queue and worker execution.

docs.title: Grounding
docs.text: The rule that the final answer may only use facts from tool results, never the model's own memory. In a regulated domain a fabricated figure that looks real is a compliance problem, so grounding is enforced by the prompt (code cannot tell where a number came from). See Step 8 · Orchestrator prompt.

docs.title: Carryover
docs.text: Reusing on a follow-up turn something an earlier turn already produced: its resolved entities, or its retrieval results in source_results. The safe form gives the model a pointer it can choose to reuse, never a pasted copy, and reuse appears as a visible plan step. See Step 8d · Carryover and the data manifest.

docs.title: Data manifest
docs.text: The [Held data] block that middleware adds to each model call: one short line per result already held in state (provenance id, success, row count, retrieval date, the question it answered). It is an index, not the data, so the model can decide to reuse a result without the rows filling its context window. See Step 8d · Carryover and the data manifest.

docs.title: Entity resolution
docs.text: Working out what a vague question refers to (turning "give me my sales" into a specific country, brand, and time period) before deciding anything else.

docs.title: run_id
docs.text: One execution attempt of a thread's work. A thread can be run more than once (an initial enqueue, a retry after a crash, a queue redelivery), and each attempt gets a fresh run_id, so logs and run-state records can tell the attempts apart. Contrast thread_id, which stays constant across all of them. See Step 4 · Identifiers that hold a run together.

docs.title: Ordinal id
docs.text: The stable position of a step within an approved plan: step 1, step 2, step 3. Unlike seq, which orders the live event stream and takes new values on replay, a step's ordinal is fixed once the plan is locked, so a report can refer to "the result of step 2" and mean the same thing on every replay. See Step 4 · Identifiers that hold a run together.

docs.title: Provenance id
docs.text: A pointer from a fact back to the tool result that produced it: which query_source call a given figure in the report came from. It makes grounding auditable: every number carries the id of its retrieval, so a reviewer, or code, can confirm no figure was invented. See Step 4 · Identifiers that hold a run together.

docs.title: owner_id
docs.text: Who proposed a plan and owns a thread. Checked on resume so one user cannot approve or resume another user's run. It is an authorization identity, not an ordering or dedup one.

docs.title: trace_id
docs.text: The observability correlation id that ties every log line, span, and model call for one request together. It exists for humans debugging after the fact; nothing in the run's correctness depends on it. Distinct from run_id, which identifies the attempt itself.

docs.title: The one distinction the whole series turns on
Transport success vs semantic success
docs.text:
Transport success means the HTTP request finished and nothing threw (200 OK). Semantic success means the right context, state, lock, plan, and persistence rules all held. A silent failure is any case where the first is true and the second is not. Every article is about one way those two can drift apart.

Missing a term? It belongs here — tell your teacher (the agent) and it will be added.

docs.title: Step 1 · State and checkpoints
docs.text:
Design question: What are the nouns and states? · Principles: Foundational Thinking, Encode Lessons in Structure

A user asks, "What were sales in France?" The agent answers with a confident, well-formatted report — about Germany. The request returned 200 OK. No error, no retry, no log line out of place. The previous question in that conversation had been about Germany, and somehow it leaked into this turn.

This is the most common silent failure in a LangGraph agent. The node logic is fine; the bug is in how state carries over between turns. To see why, you have to know the one rule that governs every value your graph stores.

Key terms (state, channel, LastValue, checkpoint) are defined once in the Glossary.

docs.title: The mental model: state is a dictionary with a rule per key
docs.text:
LangGraph state is a dictionary. What makes it different from a plain dict is that each key has a rule attached, called a channel, that decides what happens when a node writes to it.

The default rule is LastValue: the latest write replaces the previous value. That sounds harmless until you notice its other half:

If a new run does not write a key, LastValue keeps whatever the checkpoint already had.

"I did not write this key" does not mean "clear this key." It means "keep the old value." In an ordinary request handler, a variable you don't set is empty. In a checkpointed graph, a key you don't write is stale.

Here is the France/Germany bug as a state trace:

Checkpoint before the new turn
  raw_question = "sales in Germany"
  user_context = "default country: Australia"

New graph input (this turn)
  messages = ["sales in France"]

Checkpoint after the input is merged
  messages      = previous messages + ["sales in France"]
  raw_question  = "sales in Germany"            <- STALE, never rewritten
  user_context  = "default country: Australia"  <- STALE, never rewritten

The caller wrote messages and nothing else. add_messages appended the new message correctly, but raw_question and user_context still hold last turn's values, because nobody overwrote them. A downstream node reads raw_question, sees "Germany," and does exactly what it was told.

flowchart LR
    subgraph t1 ["Turn 1 — 'Germany'"]
        a1["writes:<br/>messages = [Turn 1]<br/>raw_question = Germany<br/>user_context = Australia"]
    end
    subgraph c1 ["Checkpoint after Turn 1"]
        b1["messages = [Turn 1] ✓<br/>raw_question = Germany ✓<br/>user_context = Australia ✓"]
    end
    subgraph t2 ["Turn 2 — 'France'"]
        a2["writes:<br/>messages = [Turn 2]<br/>⚠ raw_question — not written<br/>⚠ user_context — not written"]
    end
    subgraph c2 ["Checkpoint after Turn 2"]
        b2["messages = [Turn 1, Turn 2] ✓<br/>raw_question = Germany ← STALE<br/>user_context = Australia ← STALE"]
    end
    t1 --> c1 --> t2 --> c2
    style b2 fill:#fff0f0,stroke:#cc3333

The fix fits in one sentence. If a key must describe this turn, the caller must write it every turn. Everything below is how to make that discipline hard to get wrong.

Two later wrong-country bugs look the same from outside but have different causes. In Step 2, nothing is stale: a current account default outranks the country the user just typed. In Step 8, the model resolves the right country at plan time, and a default injected again after approval pulls execution back to the wrong one.

docs.title: State versus checkpoint
docs.text:
Two words that sound the same and are not:

  • State is the logical data your graph reads and writes during a run.
  • Checkpoint is the durable stored copy that lets LangGraph resume the run later, possibly in a different process after a deploy.
node returns {"plan": plan_dict}
  → LangGraph applies the channel rule for each key
    → checkpointer stores a durable snapshot
      → a later HTTP request resumes with the same thread_id
        → LangGraph reloads state from the checkpoint

A checkpoint holds more than the final visible state. During an interrupt() it also records pending writes and the interrupt payload needed to resume. That is why the stale-value problem survives across pauses, not just across turns.

There is one exception to the channel model: a human resume decision is staged as checkpoint plumbing, not as normal state. In the production approval path, the API writes (RESUME, {"type": "approve"}) into LangGraph's pending-writes area with saver.put_writes(). That value is neither LastValue nor a reducer; it is a one-shot resume value drained when the worker re-enters the paused interrupt().

docs.title: Channel types: replace versus combine
docs.text:
You choose the rule per key. There are two you will use constantly:

  • LastValue — one current value. The active plan, the current raw question. New write replaces old.
  • Reducer channels — values that should combine across writes. Message history uses add_messages so new messages append instead of replacing the whole list.
class DeepState(TypedDict):
    plan: NotRequired[dict[str, Any]]        # LastValue: replace
    entity_groups: NotRequired[list[dict[str, str]]]  # LastValue: full-list swap
    raw_question: NotRequired[str]           # LastValue: replace
    user_context: NotRequired[str]           # LastValue: replace
    messages: Annotated[list[AnyMessage], add_messages]  # reducer: append
    source_results: Annotated[list[SourceResult], operator.add]  # reducer: append
    step_status: Annotated[dict[str, str], operator.or_]  # reducer: merge

Rule of thumb: reach for LastValue only when stale carry-over is acceptable, or when every new turn is guaranteed to write an explicit replacement. If you cannot guarantee that, you have a France/Germany bug waiting to happen.

In the production deep agent, the main channels behaved like this:

State key Channel behavior Why messages add_messages reducer Conversation turns append; a new user message should not erase history. source_results operator.add reducer Each retrieval writes one result. Parallel fan-out merges losslessly, and later turns can reuse carried evidence. step_status dict merge reducer Parallel branches can update different plan steps without clobbering each other. files delta merge reducer The playbook workspace evolves over the run. plan LastValue, but sticky by design Only the gate should write it. Once locked, it must not be replaced by follow-up turns. cycle LastValue This is the turn-boundary counter that feeds plan_id. It advances only for genuinely new questions. raw_question, user_context, deep_run_id LastValue, rewritten per proposal These describe the current proposal. If they are omitted, the old proposal leaks forward. final_answer, source_cards, reported_cycle LastValue outputs The visible report is the latest delivered report for the current evidence set.

The approval decision is missing from this table on purpose. As described above, it lives in checkpoint pending writes, and the worker drains it when the paused interrupt() resumes.

docs.title: Turn the convention into an API
docs.text:
The discipline "write these keys every turn" is a convention, and conventions rot, because every new endpoint is a chance to forget one. So don't let endpoints hand-build graph input. Put the required keys behind one factory:

def build_proposal_graph_input(question: str, user_context: str) -> dict:
    return {
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        "raw_question": question,
        "user_context": user_context,
    }

The fix is the raw_question line:

"raw_question": question,

That line must run for every new user turn. Without it, the new message is appended to messages, but the old raw_question stays in the checkpoint.

Here is the bug and the fix side by side:

# BUG: only writes the chat transcript.
# raw_question silently remains whatever the previous turn wrote.
graph_input = {
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}],
}

# FIX: write every turn-scoped LastValue field on every turn.
graph_input = {
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    "raw_question": question,
    "user_context": user_context,
}

Now the convention is an API. A reviewer checks one function instead of searching every route that starts the graph, and a forgotten key becomes impossible rather than merely unlikely.

docs.title: What goes wrong
docs.text:
The problem is rarely that state is absent. Far more often, state exists but has the wrong shape, lifetime, or merge semantics. Watch for:

  • Treating an omitted key as if it clears prior state (the France/Germany bug).
  • A channel that should merge but uses LastValue, so writes clobber each other.
  • A sticky LastValue channel, such as plan, being re-persisted on a later turn even though it was minted for an older deep_run_id.
  • Confusing checkpoint pending writes with ordinary state fields. The approval decision is staged beside state so a worker can resume with no input; it should not appear in get_state().values.
  • Multiple nodes writing the same key with incompatible assumptions.
  • Mutable objects shared across parallel branches, mutated in place.
  • Channel declaration, initialization, and consumption split across unrelated files, so no one place shows the full contract.

docs.title: Guardrails for review and tests
docs.text:
• Use a clearly typed state model, and keep durable state separate from ephemeral execution metadata.
  • Review channel merge behavior as part of code review, not just the node logic.
  • Add tests that assert how state evolves across multiple node transitions, not a single call.
  • Add the test that catches this whole class: a second turn that intentionally passes empty context, asserting no value from the first turn survives.

The next step, Step 2 · Context injection, is about a specific, high-stakes case of getting values into that state: attaching the right context to the model at the right boundary, and how the wrong context, like a stale user_context above, produces an answer that looks fine and is wrong.

You should now understand

  • Why LastValue channels keep stale data when a key is not written in a new turn ("omitted ≠ cleared")
  • The difference between state (the data your graph reads and writes) and checkpoints (the durable snapshot that survives crashes and deploys)
  • How to prevent stale carry-over: every turn-scoped key must be written explicitly on every turn
  • Why a resume decision is checkpoint pending-write plumbing, not a state channel
  • Why "write required keys through one factory function" turns a convention into an API that a reviewer can check in one place
Try this

A node reads raw_question from state, uses it to query an external data source, and writes the result back to state. On turn 2, a new engineer updates the endpoint so raw_question is only included in the graph input when the user explicitly sends it. On turns where the user doesn't send it, the field is omitted. What is the failure mode, and how do you catch it in a code review?

Answer

raw_question is a LastValue channel. Omitting it on turn 2 does not clear it; it keeps the turn-1 value. The node then queries an external source with a stale question and writes a stale result to state. The response is 200 OK, the logs look clean, and the user gets an answer to a question they didn't ask. In review, ask: "Is there any path through this endpoint that omits a state key that a downstream node reads?" The answer here is yes. The fix is to make the input factory require raw_question on every call. A TypeError at startup beats a silent wrong answer in production.

docs.title: Step 2 · Context injection
docs.text:
Design question: Where are the boundaries? · Principles: Boundary Discipline

A user types: "Actually, give me sales for France." The agent replies about Australia, because somewhere before the model call your code helpfully attached "user's default country is Australia," and that injected line sat closer to the model's attention than the correction the user just typed.

The prompt looked complete. Every field was populated. The request returned 200 OK. And the answer was wrong, because the right context was attached at the wrong boundary. Context injection is one of the easiest ways to build a system that looks stable and answers incorrectly.

New to middleware, checkpoint, or state? Each term is defined once in the Glossary.

docs.title: What context injection is
docs.text:
Context injection is adding text or data to the model input that the user did not type in that exact request: user defaults, account permissions, entities and results carried over from earlier turns (carryover), retrieved documents, tool results, an approved plan.

Your code knows which parts came from memory, tools, or the user. The model does not. It sees one flat, composed prompt. Unless you label the boundaries, "trusted memory" and "the user's words" are indistinguishable to it:

Database memory
  → "User default country is Australia"

User message
  → "Give me my sales"

Injected model input (what the model sees)
  → [User context]
     User default country is Australia
     [/User context]

     Give me my sales

This is useful: "my sales" is meaningless without the account context. It is dangerous because stale or over-salient context can quietly override a later user correction, as in the France/Australia bug above. This is not Step 1's France/Germany bug, where a value left over from the last turn was read back. Here the default is current and correct. It wins only because the model weighs it above the user's correction. Step 8 adds the prompt rule that settles the precedence.

docs.title: What we assemble into each model call
docs.text:
The deep orchestrator does not send the raw message list to the model. Every model call is assembled by a chain of wrap_model_call middlewares, each of which rebuilds its slice from state and frames it onto the latest genuine human message. The framing is transient, so nothing accumulates in the checkpoint. Seven kinds of context go in and a single composed prompt comes out. One of the seven, the source catalog, rides inside the system prompt instead of going through its own middleware.

flowchart TB
    SC["Source cards / catalog<br/>what each source answers:<br/>questions · KPIs · domains · out-of-scope · relationships"]
    SP["System / orchestrator prompt<br/>plan · submit · refine · execute rules"]
    UC["[User context]<br/>persona · prior entities"]
    HD["[Held data] manifest<br/>pointers to prior results, not rows"]
    MSG["Conversation messages<br/>the running transcript"]
    TL["Tool set<br/>the 7-tool frozenset"]
    Q["User question<br/>this turn's words"]

    SC --> SP
    SP --> ASM
    UC --> ASM
    HD --> ASM
    MSG --> ASM
    TL --> ASM
    Q --> ASM

    ASM["Context assembly<br/>wrap_model_call chain · delimiters escaped"]
    ASM --> M["Model call"]
    M --> OUT["plan · tool calls · report"]

Each component has a different source, lifetime, and failure mode, which is why the prompt is assembled instead of concatenated:

Component Injected by Lifetime If it goes wrong System / orchestrator prompt base prompt (orchestrator_prompts.py) static The rules the model plans and reuses under; see Step 8 · Orchestrator prompt. Source cards / catalog within the system prompt — what each source answers: questions, KPIs, domains, out-of-scope, inter-source relationships static The model routes a step to the wrong source, attempts an out-of-scope question, or fans out redundantly; see Step 8b · Clarifications. [User context] UserContextMiddleware transient, rebuilt per call A stale value overrides a live correction (the France/Australia bug). [Held data] data manifest DataManifestMiddleware transient, rebuilt per call Inject the rows instead of the pointers and you poison the window; see Step 8d · Carryover and the data manifest. Conversation messages graph state (messages) durable, delta-checkpointed Attach context to a synthetic summary message instead of the user's; see below. Tool set AllowedToolsMiddleware per call The model reaches for a tool that isn't structurally reachable; see Middleware. User question framed onto the latest HumanMessage this turn Framed onto the wrong (synthetic) message, or the injected text forges the closing delimiter; both are covered next.

The two transient blocks ([User context] and [Held data]) are the riskiest, because they are user-influenced and re-composed every turn. Both are wrapped in delimited blocks, and both must escape their own closing tag so held text cannot forge the boundary. The rest of this chapter covers that discipline.

docs.title: Two ways it goes wrong
docs.text:
Most context-injection bugs come from attaching the context to the wrong thing, not from forgetting it. Two common ones:

1. Attaching context to a synthetic message, not the user's. Some frameworks insert synthetic messages during history summarization. They may still be HumanMessage objects, but they are not user-authored. If you blindly compose context onto "the last human message," you may be labeling a machine-written summary as the user's latest words. Walk back to the real one:

for i in range(len(messages) - 1, -1, -1):
    msg = messages[i]

    if not isinstance(msg, HumanMessage):
        continue

    if msg.additional_kwargs.get("lc_source") == "summarization":
        continue  # framework-created, not the user

    messages[i] = HumanMessage(
        content=compose_with_context(msg.content, context),
        additional_kwargs=msg.additional_kwargs,
    )
    break

2. Not escaping your own delimiter. Your format uses [/User context] to close the trusted block. The text inside that block comes partly from the user's prior conversation history, which you do not fully control. If any of that history contains the literal string [/User context], it will close the block early, and the text after it will look to the model like it is outside the trusted section.

Here is what the model sees when that happens:

WITHOUT ESCAPING — what the model sees:

  [User context]                         ← trusted block opens
  Prior notes: I want Australia data.
